entries.title: ‘A Certain Grain of Stupidity’

entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

In 1961, on a barrier island off the coast of Georgia, Eleanor “Sandy” Torrey West and her husband founded a residency, the Ossabaw Island Project (OIP). As Christopher Alessandrini writes in our October 8 issue, the island—which West had inherited from her patrician parents—was “a patchwork landscape of salt marshes and maritime forests, tidal creeks and interdune meadows, feral hogs and plovers, lofty cabbage palms and live oaks hung with portieres of Spanish moss.” It was the perfect setting for what became, alongside Genesis, a sister program founded there a decade later, a “multidisciplinary retreat” for a “Who’s Who of twentieth-century American cultural history,” including writers and artists like Ralph Ellison and Sally Mann, as well as “scientists, historians, literary theorists, naturalists, religious leaders, philosophers, businesspeople, and anthropologists.”

Alessandrini is a managing editor in the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s digital department. His writing has appeared in, among other places, Frieze, The Brooklyn Rail, Interview, and the anthology Points of View: 100 Connections to Art (2026) from Yale University Press. For the Review, he has also written about the painter Louis Fratino, the photographer Graciela Iturbide, and Felipe Baeza’s collages.

This week I wrote to Alessandrini to ask him about his trip to Savannah, the development of taste, and the seductions of fiction.

Nandini Krishnan: How did you first encounter the Ossabaw residencies? Did you get to go to Ossabaw on one of the limited appointments or research trips they allow?

Christopher Alessandrini: I first learned about Ossabaw Island while I was writing a short story about the artist Philip Guston. I was reading his daughter’s memoir, Night Studio (1988), when I came across the name in a passage about his wife, Musa McKim, a painter turned poet who in many ways supported his life and work. As I write in my essay, Musa asserted her selfhood in the relationship with occasional “vacations” from Guston—a phrase both of them used to describe the periods when she would simply take leave of their life together. Sometimes she would be gone for a brief window; other times for more extended periods, like her two-week residency on Ossabaw in 1974. (His letter, which is quoted in the review, shows him spiraling a bit in her absence.)

Unfortunately, I didn’t have an opportunity to visit Ossabaw while I was in Savannah. (I did, however, encounter Maya Hawke’s stunt double at the Flannery O’Connor Childhood Home Museum.) Everyone told me if I asked around, before long I’d find someone chartering a boat to Ossabaw. I was skeptical—but it almost happened! There was an expedition slated for the day of my flight back to New York. I had a travel grant from the Rabkin Foundation—which more art critics should know about—but the budget was too tight to change my itinerary at the last minute. And maybe some foolish part of me had decided ahead of time that it was more romantic not to see Ossabaw before writing the review.

I am, however, heading back to Savannah in October as a guest lecturer at Savannah College of Art and Design, to discuss art criticism and my job working on digital interpretive media at the Met. I’m hopeful that something will work out this time around.

Is Guston’s art important to you? What about his life and work do you connect with?

The story I wrote, “Maverick Road,” exists thanks entirely to a kind and open-ended invitation from the book’s coeditor Emmie Francis, who had the inspired idea to commission five short stories about Philip Guston for a collection put out by Printed Matter.

I’d been asked to write about him before, for a more straightforward exhibition review, but I’d declined the opportunity. In a strange reversal, fiction offered me more critical distance than a review might have, and it also allowed me to forge my own relationship with Guston. I didn’t feel any pressure to become an authority on his practice, which was tremendously liberating, although the process was arguably more intense than if I’d simply done the review. I was steeped in the Guston menagerie for long enough that his motifs began to seep into and populate my own life. And I found that they entered the story more organically this way, too, almost of their own volition. I set the story upstate—a naive young couple moves to Woodstock while producing a film on Guston—and gave it lightly gothic undertones, along with a soundtrack sourced largely from Girl, Interrupted.

Many people look to Guston as this art-world maverick: a prodigy who pulled from Giorgio de Chirico and Krazy Kat in equal measure, was high school friends with Jackson Pollock, drew inspiration from the Mexican muralists for some very sincere social-realist tableaux under the Works Progress Administration, and entered into abstraction before breaking with its apolitical posturing to summon a new visual language to try to address his own vexed relationship with contemporary life. The controversial turn toward figuration cost him many friendships in the art world and led, in part, to his self-imposed exile in Woodstock. He had every incentive to continue in lockstep with the anointed boy-gods of Abstract Expressionism and yet he strayed. I admire his bravery and stubbornness.

Advertisement

What actually moved me to write the story, beyond a vague political respect, was the cyclical nature of Guston’s obsessions: how he fixated on certain motifs and forms over and over again. It’s almost like he was cursed with a beautiful glitch, this uncanny inability to move beyond a few tropes and “common objects”—his lightbulbs and books, clocks and half-drawn shades, teapots and picture frames and hooded figures. They could disappear for decades, seemingly tamed or submerged in the depths of his consciousness, but they inevitably resurfaced. And each time he reimagined these forms, he had to forge a new syntax to accommodate a changed worldview and political consciousness: his new vision of reality, or the reality of his new vision.

He can’t outrun himself in the end. It’s like what F. Scott Fitzgerald said about how writers only have two or three stories in them, which they recite over and over, “each time in a new disguise.” That’s sort of how I feel about Guston—and, as I get older, I start to realize it might be true of me. Perhaps better to make peace with that early and get on with it.

Do you think the new residencies starting up this year at Ossabaw will be able to recapture the mythological, “primordial…drama of humanity’s entanglement with the natural world,” as you write, that characterized the old programs?

I certainly hope they can capture some of the early incarnations’ magic—though I suspect the goal is different now. When the Wests started the OIP and Genesis in the 1960s and 1970s, they were the first of their kind on the island. So much of their freewheeling spirit, I think, is attributable to the fact that they were unprecedented—pure experiments in communal living and making in the “primordial” wilderness.

One of the components that I’d most like to see replicated—both on Ossabaw and, more broadly, in the arts—is the Wests’ insistence on two principles. First is the love of interdisciplinarity. As the child of an architect and an immunologist, I’ve grown up thinking about how cross-pollination works. My entire theory of writing is indebted to looking at floor plans with my mother as a child—which gave me the sense of language as something spatial and inhabitable.

The second principle was a commitment to freedom from the pressure to produce. Today it seems like every opportunity, either in the creative world or elsewhere, demands some kind of “deliverable” or outcome. And the results are often underwhelming. Pressure can be galvanizing, of course, but it can also warp the artistic process and remove some of the magic that might have attended a more organic timeline. I think the Wests were entirely correct to insist that creativity is fickle and unpredictable. Art and ideas take time to gestate; they have an inner logic or rhythm that doesn’t necessarily map onto contemporary models of productivity.

This essay focuses in part on the creative process and sources of artistic inspiration. What about particular exhibitions, artworks, or artists (like Louis Fratino or Felipe Baeza) inspires you to want to write about them?

This may sound strange, but I’m always looking for a certain thickness when I look at art. Sometimes it’s a particularly dense or heavy surface, a sense of depth and texture, a sensuous handling of material. Sometimes it’s a density of intertextual allusion or a layered sense of history. Sometimes it’s just that I perceive a certain quality of attention or concentration captured in the work—almost like I’m responding to the record of time and focus that the artist spent making it, a kind of correspondence. That spark of creation (or whatever you want to call it) that’s transmitted across time.

I’ve also realized that I’m fond of artists who are at home in art history—or rather, they have the patience and humility to search through it, like magpies, to find their kindred spirits. Nancy Spero made stencils of women from history and literature and turned them into a theater troupe to enact her paper scrolls. Fratino and Baeza are both artists conversant in art history—although their sources of inspiration are heterogeneous and surprising, and often fall beyond the visual record. I always get the sense that their work is driven by memory, desire, affinity.

Advertisement

I didn’t study art history as an undergraduate, though I spent a good deal of my childhood in museums and reading art books—which is why I have a particular fondness for exhibition catalogs and the much-derided coffee-table book. My arts education was patchwork at best, driven mostly by curiosity and instinct, so it’s sometimes difficult to articulate why, exactly, a particular artist’s work appeals to me. It’s like how birdwatchers claim to have a “spark bird,” the species that initiated them into the hobby: there’s always a work that catches my eye and suggests that something beyond its immediate allure will sustain and reward my attention. I’ve learned to trust it over the years.

When did you first develop an interest in art criticism? Was there ever a period where you were interested in making art?

The first short story I ever published was in high school, in a literary magazine for teen writing called Polyphony H.S. based out of Chicago. It was a stilted ekphrastic vignette based on Edward Hopper’s painting Room in New York (1932)—a very literal transcription of the scene, painfully sincere and realist. I continued publishing short fiction, mostly in that same earnest vein, though in college I think it developed more of an edge. I almost pursued an MFA in fiction at the University of Michigan, but instead I worked at a literary magazine and then went on a fellowship to Berlin and Mount Athos. I was working on a novella about life in a monastery, inspired by Simonopetra. When I moved to Brooklyn to live with my then partner, who was also a writer, I decided to apply for a job working at the front desk of the Met Breuer, which at the time was housed in the former Whitney building on Madison Avenue. I spent my days under that extraordinary field of lobby lights. That’s when everything shifted.

There were so many people at the museum who took me under their wings, or who taught me about the fabric of art history: how it’s made, its internal battles, how shifting schemes of valuation affect the circulation of images and objects, how meaning is made personally and collectively. I worked with Andrea Bayer and Laura D. Corey on the audio guide for Making the Met, 1870–2020, narrated by Steve Martin. I also started wandering the nearby galleries during lunch with a fellow editor in my department, Will Fenstermaker, a talented arts writer who introduced me to the small-gallery scene and showed me how the entire art ecosystem was interconnected, as did Marina Ruiz Molina, a paper conservator and dear friend who always guides me toward the most interesting subjects. (Recently, she’s been involved in work around the archive of the downtown artist Sheyla Baykal at Soft Network.) And with my co-conspirators, Stephanie Wuertz, a filmmaker and puppeteer, and Robin Schwalb, a textile artist and audiovisual specialist, I coproduced an archival-film series called From the Vaults, which expanded my interests in documentary filmmaking and the genre of the film essay, which has a lot of crossover with arts writing.  

How different is the process of writing fiction from that of writing nonfiction?

That Guston story was the first piece of fiction I’d published since graduating from college. (There are lots of others I’ve written, of course, but none that I want in circulation just yet.) It’s a strange one, a bit uneven, like something concocted in a petri dish under the hood of night. There are moments that I look back on fondly, where I can almost recall the spirit of inspiration that allowed certain unusual combinations of images to swarm together. Those are the best parts, when the language hits a brisk stride and conjures its own momentum—and I feel this way about writing both fiction and nonfiction.

Getting there, though, is a truly unconscious process. Flannery O’Connor, that patron saint of Savannah, said that all fiction writers need “a certain grain of stupidity.” I’ve always found my best work comes when the intellect—which might have served as some kind of scaffold—is breached somehow and falls away. It’s not stupidity that takes over so much as raw instinct and nerve, lightly feral. You don’t know how it’s going to behave or what’s going to happen. Wilderness, like creativity, is entirely unpredictable—and like Ossabaw, it probably needs to remain fairly undeveloped in order to flourish. The Wests understood that those long stretches of boredom, where it seems like nothing is happening, are the golden hours. When the mind clears its channels and keeps the gears turning. A low and steady hum.

The difference between the two forms, for me, comes down to the degree of vulnerability involved in publication. This is probably my own naiveté, but nonfiction feels less exposed somehow. Of course, I’m showing my cards by deciding which shows I decide to cover, how I spread my attention: my taste is on display through what I decide to notice or defend or critique publicly.

Fiction always feels like it has a higher potential for embarrassment, because you’re trying to sustain an illusion, to hold someone’s attention over a prolonged period of time when the entire thing is an act of imagination. And that’s not even covering the mechanics: it can’t all move at the same rhythm or operate in the same register, otherwise it becomes inert. Any process of seduction is dynamic. A single word can break the spell.

It’s not that nonfiction doesn’t seduce, either. But sometimes I find that because it’s not spending every word trying to convince you of its own reality, it can occasionally coast on the confidence that it’s relaying necessary information. A piece of nonfiction needs to function in a certain way—factual accuracy is important, for example—and to convey certain points. Those can give it structural integrity. Fiction has its own logic, too, which is often quite intricate. It depends entirely on the story at hand—which you, as the writer, can determine. In the end it’s up to you and how successfully you manage your unreality. But you also need to remember, of course, that you’ve invited someone else along for the ride.

entries.title: Nothing Stays Buried
entries.summary: Nancy Lemann sets her sad screwball novels of manners in the closed-off world of upper-crust white New Orleans that she grew up in.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
“There are just three big cities in the United States that are ‘story cities’—New York, of course, New Orleans, and, best of the lot, San Francisco.” The line is Frank Norris’s, but it’s better known as the epigraph of O. Henry’s “A Municipal Report” (1909), the municipality being Nashville, as if chosen to prove Norris wrong. Well, New York—of course. San Francisco I’m not so sure about. It’s better in the movies, even if Vertigo was based on a French thriller, and as for the rest of the country, Norris couldn’t have predicted how Chicago would develop, much less Los Angeles.

But New Orleans is a different matter. It really is a “story city,” and not just because it too is a port with a complicated racial history, the most complicated, in the early days, of any American entrepôt. It’s the city where George Washington Cable set “The ‘Haunted House’ in Royal Street” (1889), about a mysterious French Quarter beauty in the 1830s who got so much pleasure out of torturing her slaves that even the antebellum world knew horror. It’s Kate Chopin’s city too, the home of The Awakening, and also the place where William Faulkner found his voice and then set the eeriest chapters of Absalom, Absalom!

I know it only as a reader and a tourist. But speaking as a reader, it does seem that nothing stays buried in New Orleans, and not just because the graves in its fabled flood-prone cemeteries are all above ground. Lost histories become legible, and in the immediate aftermath of World War II Tennessee Williams’s A Streetcar Named Desire provided an unforgettable picture of the town’s vigor and decay, while Robert Penn Warren used the charm and corruption of the entire state of Louisiana as the stage for All the King’s Men.

Still, those aren’t the only stories the city has to tell. Everybody’s a sinner in the land where the saints go marching in, but some people do it in seersucker and pearls, and upper-crust white New Orleans has been the setting for some superb novels of manners, fine-grained accounts of a closed-off world. Three or four families in a country village, Jane Austen said in defining her subject, but make it five or six in the Uptown neighborhoods, where the city seems small enough to be knowable, and then build a sense of pressure from the world outside. That’s the terrain of Walker Percy’s The Moviegoer and of Elizabeth Spencer’s The Snare, whose title refers to the city itself. And it is also the world of Percy’s disciple Nancy Lemann, whose two sad screwball comedies of the 1980s are now back in print, accompanied by The Oyster Diaries, her first new book in more than twenty years.

Lives of the Saints, first published in 1985, makes no explicit reference to the old song, familiar from football games and funerals alike, and yet it’s everywhere felt in the syncopation of Lemann’s prose. It’s been a long time since I read a novel whose language seemed so engagingly mannered or from which I wanted to quote so much. It starts with a wedding that its narrator, the mousily named Louise Brown, describes as one where

everyone had breakdowns…including the bride and groom. Especially the bride and groom. Crowded parties like at the Stewarts’ often can be known to Bring on Breakdowns. Especially if the Stewarts are the hosts.

Repetitive? No. Let’s call it reiteration, an amplification that seems less linguistic than rhythmic, sonic, even musical. Including the bride and groom. Now hit that phrase again but make it louder, let us hear those horns. Especially the bride and groom. Or maybe Lemann will bend a note, shift its grammar a bit. One of her characters has the habit of “shredding napkins, matchbooks, and cigarette packages” and goes on to fill “about three ashtrays with shreddings.” That s makes the verb a noun; the word doubles itself, and in the same sentence too.

The groom’s breakdown makes him scream for other women, the bride’s makes her want to go off with another man, and everyone without exception is drunk and “unglued.” They’re having multiple breakdowns, one right after another, they’re cracking up, they glue themselves together again only so that they can break down once more, and this is entirely accepted and normal on a “sweltering April night” in New Orleans. All in all, it’s “one of the worst events in my experience, tragic in society.” Not tragic, but “tragic in society,” in the particular part of society that calls itself society, where people shriek with delight and dismay and no one can tell the difference. It’s a voice—Louise’s, or Lemann’s—that undercuts its own hyperbole and yet allows for it, too: an attitude summed up by what’s described as “the mock-amazed congeniality of New Orleanians confronted with the spectacle of one another.” That amazement is a put-on. The congeniality is real.

Advertisement

The wedding guests include everyone Louise has ever known, “plus a party of out-of-towners whose broad Memphis and Charleston accents shocked me, although we were the same, Americans far from that hub of the universe along the East Coast.” The same? Perhaps to people from Boston, who can’t hear the difference between those shockingly different Deep South accents. But to Louise herself, who can hear it? There’s a hall-of-mirrors quality to this southern schtick, a deliberately unsettled point of view in which every statement seems both true and false at once, and clichés are the writer’s best friend. So Louise announces that “southerners need carbonation” as an accident-prone little boy sits “swilling Cokes” after a visit to the emergency room, while “youthful folly” has its season in New Orleans, and “its season is youth.” The napkin shredder at the wedding tells her that her slip is showing and then says that it reminds him of the South. At which point this New Englander knows that there’s a joke in there somewhere and hopes it’s not on him.

It’s a young person’s book—Lemann wasn’t yet thirty when it appeared—and reading it now I wonder how it would have struck me if I’d read it then, back when I was young myself. I doubt I would have heard so much in it, though I would have recognized its “wastrel-youth contingent” as a version of Evelyn Waugh’s bright young people; Lemann’s epigraph comes from Waugh’s autobiography, and I too was steeped in his fictional world. But there are other echoes of that dandy tradition here as well, hints of Wilde, of Eliot’s Prufrock, and also of Nancy Mitford. Delery Anhalt, the narrator of The Oyster Diaries, speaks of her own “rabid Anglophilia,” and despite its regional specificity Lives of the Saints owes more in formal terms to those brittle English models than it does to American ones. What separates it from them, and from Waugh’s books especially, is its sweetness.

That sweetness is a function of its faith, and by that I don’t mean anything as simple as religious belief. Waugh was thrilled and appalled by the world he created in books like Vile Bodies, and more than half hated the people he put into them. Lemann isn’t in the least appalled, and more than half loves the ones she puts into hers. Many of them are absurd. Mrs. Stewart, the mother of that errant bride, likes nothing more than to “spend an entire afternoon talking about what hat she wore when she was fifteen,” and in that she is rivaled by her mother-in-law, who enjoys remembering the “shoe sizes her friends wore in 1910.” Yet these are the absurdities of Austen’s Miss Bates, not of Waugh’s merciless Margot Metroland. The two Mrs. Stewarts belong to a world that Lemann takes for granted, however keen her irony, and the faith in Lives of the Saints has to do with her city’s ready acceptance of “youthful folly,” and with what lies beyond it.

For Louise the best part of that wedding comes when the napkin shredder, a young man named Claude Collier, “turned my collar down and called me Darling.” Nothing so strange about that, everyone here calls other people Darling, and yet the tenderness with which he does it shocks her even more than those accents. It feels “uncharacteristic. I had known him for so many years,” and it surprises her into something like love. At some undefined point that love seems to become sexual, but what matters more is that these two stand as the essential witnesses to each other’s life. Claude needs that. He is kindness personified, somebody other people love because he looks so fascinated by everything they do. But in his late twenties he is not, his father says, “using his abilities.” He drinks three cocktails “in the time that it took me to drink one”; he never finished college, doesn’t work at anything much, and seems instead to have made a career of solicitousness, attending to others but never himself. He is at once brilliant and unbookish, and professes to be mystified when people find him strange. Nobody believes him when he says he’s just “normal,” and reading about him made me remember a line from The Moviegoer in which a young woman is described as possessing “an antic sort of seriousness, which is not seriousness at all but despair masquerading as seriousness.”

Advertisement

That’s Claude. Is it also Louise? Is she only a witness, or do her observations mask some crisis of her own? She tells us very little about herself and seems essentially without parents; instead she’s as absorbed with Claude as he is with everyone else. Or absorbed, rather, by her concern for his entire family. There’s his father, a federal judge and amateur classicist named St. Louis Collier, and his much younger brother, also called St. Louis, the one known as Louis and the other as Saint. Louis, Louise—she could be the family’s missing daughter. Claude’s mother, meanwhile, is a “Yankee girl” Mr. Collier met at Harvard who has come down to New Orleans as to an alien land, a world of carnival balls and ebullient ossified tradition. “A stern calm” dominates her relations with her husband; something has happened there, though Louise doesn’t quite know what. She knows only that Mrs. Collier expects the worst, and about halfway through that worst will come.

A dark comedy, an alcohol-soaked idyll. And yet there is faith indeed, and trust. Not belief, not a quest for certainty, but a search for purpose and meaning that derives from Percy, who suggests that such a search might in itself be purpose enough. Youthful folly has its season, but in New Orleans that season is like the heat, and goes on longer than anywhere else. Seasons do change, however, and this reader at least suspends his disbelief. Claude finds something he cares about doing, for a while at least. He begins to use his talents, and yet to Louise he remains embroiled in “shady things…which did not fit into his character.” But they do, and on the novel’s last page he says that though he’s “not the person you portray,” it does matter that she sees him that way. “You are my heart,” this damaged saint tells our suddenly unreliable narrator, and then he turns down Bourbon Street and disappears.

That ending pulls the novel together, but for much of its length it appears as aimless as a pub crawl, a series of well-honed sketches of New Orleans life. On Sunday evenings Mr. Collier lights six cigars and with three “lodged…between the fingers” of each hand retreats to his library; a young lawyer at the firm where Louise works as a typist interrupts a mailroom conversation to ask what she would do “if your dog had rabies because it wasn’t blessed.”

Lemann’s one book of nonfiction, The Ritz of the Bayou (1987), which grew out of a failed assignment for Vanity Fair, is even more piercingly observed. In his introduction to this new edition James Wolcott recalls once hearing her fret about the difficulties of plot, and she was probably right to. She has an eye and an ear but not a conventional sense of structure, and when the magazine sent the young novelist to cover the 1985 criminal trial of Louisiana’s governor Edwin Edwards, she couldn’t manage to make the charges against him seem clear. She does name them—“racketeering, fraud, and bribery”—and notes that they involved hospitals and Las Vegas alike. But the details are impossible to follow, though in fairness many of Edwards’s co-conspirators didn’t understand them either. Vanity Fair killed the story; that didn’t stop Knopf from taking it on.

As a piece of journalism The Ritz of the Bayou stands as a kissing cousin to Hunter S. Thompson. Edwards was then in his third of four terms, and outside the state he is best remembered for his openly crooked honesty; during one campaign he boasted that the only way he could lose “is if I’m caught in bed with either a dead girl or a live boy.” His trial had a lot of “human frailty floating around,” and that, Lemann writes, is the sort of thing that puts “my ticker…back in business.”

Her account is at least as concerned with her own ticker as it is with the trial, and yet it also holds a place in a curious line of books about Louisiana’s governors. There’s Warren’s All the King’s Men, which turned Huey Long into an extraordinary character called Willie Stark, showing where he came from and why he rose and fell. That’s tragedy, both on the page and in historical fact as well. Some years after his assassination Long’s younger brother Earl was also elected to that office, a man who once said that if the state’s people ever got good government they wouldn’t like it. Late in life he traveled with the stripper Blaze Starr and became the posthumous subject of A.J. Liebling’s vividly reported The Earl of Louisiana (1961). That’s farce. The self-described “lizard” Edwards—and The Ritz of the Bayou itself—are whatever comes after farce. The state suffered; the prose didn’t.

The trial was held in federal court in New Orleans, and for Lemann it is all theatrics and mood. The book is only loosely chronological and written in “short spurts or vignettes,” most of them under a page in length—a snatch of overheard conversation, a paragraph of rumor, a comment on the local oysters. She rides in an elevator with Edwards, who tells her she’s too pretty to be a reporter; she observes his perpetually “joshing” clan of hangers-on, notes the never-understated clothing of his wife and daughter, and ends by developing a crush on an elderly defense lawyer. Sometimes she quotes the commentary of a dry-witted figure she calls the “courtroom existentialist,” and at night she sits over cocktails with her fellow journalists in the bar at the Lafayette Hotel. Lemann is more or less convinced that Edwards is guilty, but nobody is surprised when it all ends first in a mistrial and later an acquittal. People in Louisiana have been doing business this way for a long time; they know how to “live with themselves,” and truth is a relative term.

It’s certainly not anything the trial itself provides, though at the turn of the millennium Edwards did find himself in jail on a set of other charges. What becomes clear, however, is that the trial stands as Lemann’s pretext for sorting out her relation to the world from which she came. Not that her own slice of Louisiana has much in common with the governor’s. He’s country, a hardscrabble Cajun populist. She’s city and educated, a well-off New Orleanian who is also at home in New York, and sometimes the snobbery shows. Just where does she fit? She loves the South’s green heat, but is there a place for her in it? Where and who and with whom does she want to be? Yet Lemann tells us almost nothing about her own circumstances; the questions hang, and the book is marked instead by a sharp sense of the unspoken.

Still, we do eventually realize that the courtroom existentialist is a member of her own family, and that she’s in love. The voice on the other end of her frequent phone calls has a Boston accent, but it isn’t going well, and at a certain point she leaves the trial behind and drives two hundred miles to the hotel of her title in order to face a set of her own undescribed “sorrows,” troubles bad enough to make her feel that “I too was cracking up.” The Ritz of the Bayou is very funny, and a lot of its comedy comes from the same kind of reiterative drumbeat that characterizes Lives of the Saints. She writes that “the juror who has blackouts had a blackout and we had to adjourn for the day,” and at one point she repeats the phrase “human frailty” six times in three short paragraphs, which really does convince you that there’s a lot of it floating around down there. But the book’s center, its emotional ballast, isn’t finally in that courtroom, and what sticks with me is her own frailty, and her strength too, the strength that allows for the care and craft behind this picture of a narrator on the edge.

Lives of the Saints was first published by Knopf and then kept in print for years by the Louisiana State University Press, part of a handsome line of trade paperbacks called Voices of the South. It has always had its readers, but the three novels that followed were not so lucky, and they remain hard to find. Sportsman’s Paradise (1992) and Malaise (2002) concern displaced southerners—New York, California—while the third, The Fiery Pantheon (1999), begins at a grand hotel in the Virginia mountains and draws on some of the same families as Lives of the Saints. The latter’s reappearance in company with a new novel has produced its share of profiles and reviews, but nothing I’ve read has said much about its author’s long silence; maybe that gap between books is just something to note, and no more. The Oyster Diaries does, however, present me with a peculiar set of qualms and scruples. Lemann’s brother, the historian and journalist Nicholas Lemann, has a book of his own out this spring, a memoir called Returning.1 It describes their family’s long history in Louisiana, from an ancestor’s arrival in 1836 as a peddler from Germany, a typical business for Jewish immigrants of the time, through the decades of steadily rising fortune that culminated in the legal career of the siblings’ rigorously nonobservant father, Thomas, and finally Nicholas’s return to a life of Jewish practice. The book is genuinely informative about both the South and the history of American Judaism, and I wish I had not read it.

As writers the siblings don’t seem to share much. His prose is the journalist’s classic windowpane; hers is anything but. She finds her guide to their story city in Walker Percy; he takes his cues from All the King’s Men and on the page is far more concerned with race and the legacy of slavery. But the two of them do share a common formation, a set of family tales, of secrets and silences, and in reading it’s hard to forget all that, however much I try. It’s one thing to note the links between Nancy Lemann’s own books. Claude Collier returns in the new one, for example, and she traces out his later and still-disheveled life. That includes a brief marriage to Louise, who has exchanged her own nominal Judaism for a set of “saintly Catholic ways.” Which doesn’t necessarily mean she’s a Catholic. Delery’s father is a scholarly lawyer devoted to the study of Latin grammar, and in extreme old age he begins to unravel the cigars he’s now forbidden to smoke. Earlier on, however, he spends years on a diary that rates and records the oysters he eats each day for lunch; so too does the courtroom existentialist in The Ritz of the Bayou. But when I read in Returning of a once-inexplicable coolness in the marriage of the Lemann parents, and then match it up to that of the Colliers’ marriage in Lives of the Saints, and again to Delery’s parents in the new book, adding in Thomas Lemann’s own well-documented oyster habit…well, I’d rather not.2

So let’s bracket it. Lemann has always drawn on her own biography, but let’s not go down that intertextual rabbit hole; let’s refuse the so often self-serious game of peekaboo that autofiction plays with the reader, daring you to confuse author and narrator, daring you not to. It’s “annoying,” to borrow one of this narrator’s favorite words, even though Lemann herself is tempted by it. Why else would she give Delery two brothers instead of the one she actually has? But that veil seems too transparent to distract us much, and in both its humor and its tight-lipped asperity that very word, “annoying,” is enough to suggest a way around the problem. Neither of those qualities is one that I associate with the genre’s most regular practitioners, and I’m going to try instead to characterize The Oyster Diaries as it might appear to a reader who comes to it clean, maybe having read Lives of the Saints but no more.

The style has kept the same rhythms, but after almost forty years it’s grown a bit blunter. Lemann’s early narrators were flippant; this one is ticked off. She’s impatient too, performs impatience, rather, an impatience with the way things are and the way they go on and on without ever getting any better. I don’t have time for this, she seems to say, and yet Delery also likes the aggravation, or at least she likes Kierkegaard, who is “everything I adore: he’s in a bad mood, everything annoys him, and he is not afraid to repeat himself.”

The book’s opening pages appear unstudied in the way that comes only after a great deal of work, a tartly phrased “Diary of Remorse,” remorse being a “more violent” emotion than mere regret. In her volunteer job at the criminal court Delery finds herself “madly defending” a man who exposed himself, which makes one of her daughters say that she has “Stockholm syndrome for the patriarchy.” That’s a pang, and she also keeps a list of her own faults; she’s self-absorbed, heartless, boring, lazy, unkind, and obsessed with criticizing her in-laws. More remorse, and yet for her that emotion has one cause above all: New Orleans itself, “because I don’t live there now.” Being away from it makes her feel as though her heart’s in lockdown, and with that, Delery says, “the tragedies begin.”

Those tragedies include her mother’s early death and many years later her father’s. She has long since made peace with his second marriage, to a woman just a few years older than she is, but while “my mother had been a force to be reckoned with…my stepmother was a force that could not be reckoned with,” and she finds it hard to recognize that the necessary decisions about his last illness and care are not fully hers to make. Then there’s some trouble in her own marriage, which sends her back to Shakespeare, seeking a guide to villainy. She has, she thinks, been too innocent, a “quixotic” delusory innocence, and that makes her remember the boys she dated in her twenties, who “each… broke my heart, each one in a different yet hauntingly similar way.” Yet as she streams a production of Don Giovanni she feels bereft when Mozart’s character goes down at the end to hell—a cad, sure, but one who still makes that ticker “beat faster.”

It will all finish with her soul properly “calibrated” at last, and in reading I had a pair of not quite conflicting thoughts. The first was that I’m not sure this is a novel. The second is that it doesn’t matter. The Oyster Diaries is made up of eight free-standing sections, each presented in the kind of “short spurts”—a paragraph, a page—that characterize her other work. They reinforce and build on one another, and yet they aren’t precisely chapters; I wouldn’t recommend taking them in any other order than the one Lemann has given them, but almost all of them could be read on their own. The only one that seems like a conventional story is called “Love in the Ruins”—Percy again—and starts with what she describes as a typically New Orleans “narrow escape,” a traffic accident “beneath the green arcade of oaks,” before going on to detail the later life of Claude and Louise. The rhetorical register of the others is far closer to that of the essay—digressive, reminiscent, even ruminative—while the concluding “Lions and Daughters” begins like a glossy travel piece before veering into an unnerving minor key.

So, not a novel, as Handel’s Water Music is not a symphony. It is instead a suite of prose dances, of more-or-less fictional moments. What matters more than any such question of category is that this mind is on every page an interesting place to be. Not a comfortable one, never that; there’s no comfort to be found in someone who tells us that while “self-loathing is bad…there is a fine line between self-loathing and self-awareness.” But interesting, whether that mind belongs to Delery Anhalt or to Nancy Lemann herself.

entries.title: De Kooning Draws a Picture
entries.summary: Willem de Kooning's works on paper document his efforts to find ways of retaining both image and abstraction, depth and flatness.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
These people don’t know what they’re talking about, but I do! That was the message—the kind that often presages a new critic—from the twenty-nine-year-old painter Elaine de Kooning to Thomas B. Hess, the twenty-seven-year-old managing editor of ART news, in 1948. Founded in 1902, the magazine was primarily devoted to art historical essays and reports on old master acquisitions, while dutifully neglecting new developments in its hometown of New York City. Hess had studied at Yale, specializing in French art history, and was knowledgeable about a lineage of criticism stretching from the salon reviews of Denis Diderot to poet-critics like Charles Baudelaire writing within densely constellated scenes. After two years at ART news, he was starting to feel the electricity emanating from artists’ studios downtown and wanted to hear her out.

In 1948 de Kooning was a decade into her relationship with her husband, Willem de Kooning, and at the center of a cyclone of making and talking and looking that engulfed New York artists of the 1930s and 1940s, from Arshile Gorky to Franz Kline. She had studied with Hans Hofmann in Provincetown and with Josef Albers at Black Mountain College. She attended dance performances with her neighbor Edwin Denby and discussed his reviews—which rank among the finest criticism of the period—as he wrote them, measuring her perceptions against his and seeing how writing on deadline gets done, and she was ready to undertake her own. Yet a critic who was also an artist, and furthermore the wife of an artist, presented an ethical problem. The New York art world was small. Wouldn’t she just flatter her subjects? They’re all my friends, she reassured Hess. “I know everybody. So, there’s no possibility of favoritism.” De Kooning became the first artist writing criticism for ART news at the moment it was poised to become the most important publication in American art.

What bonded Hess and Elaine de Kooning above all was a deep conviction that Willem de Kooning was the greatest living painter (perhaps allowing “American” as the only qualification until Picasso’s death in 1973). Hess wrote a number of reviews of his shows, articles and the first monograph on his work in 1959, and the catalog for the first retrospective, which he curated at MoMA in 1968 and which traveled internationally. These writings are suffused with quotations from de Kooning about his ideas and detailed descriptions of how his works were made. For her part, Elaine was a zealous and charismatic proselytizer. She, Hess, and their close friend the critic Harold Rosenberg—a formidable triumvirate—became Willem’s chief champions. (Both men were also Elaine’s lovers, which does not seem to have adversely affected their relationships with her husband or each other.)

In 1949 Hess debuted the “Paints a Picture” series: long, heavily illustrated profiles that followed an artist creating a single work from beginning to end. The format often underscored that making art was not reducible to a formula, something conceptualized and then executed. Rather, it was a mysterious unfolding: at every moment the process was subject to examination, reflection, and alteration, imbuing the object with the intelligence of its maker. Elaine’s hands-on knowledge of materials and process, as well as her comfort in the studio, made her well prepared to write this kind of essay; in the first years she was responsible for most of them, on everything from tempera paintings by Andrew Wyeth to steel sculptures by David Smith.

The “Paints a Picture” format proved highly adaptable during its twenty-year run, but above all it was ideal for explicating the formal and conceptual operations of Willem de Kooning. In “De Kooning Paints a Picture” (1953), Hess reconstructs the “vacillating, Hamlet-like history” of one of the defining works of postwar art: Woman I (1950–1953). His account details de Kooning’s year and a half of continuous work on the painting beginning in the spring of 1950, after which it was put away and new Woman paintings were embarked upon; then it was restretched and slightly altered, the artist never satisfied, until, as Hess puts it, “Woman escaped by truck from its creator” to be exhibited in 1953.

Hess renounces a linear progression in favor of cyclical struggle, in the making of the painting and also in art history more generally. Despite its appearance of having been painted at great speed, which seemed to bespeak Romantic self-expression, Woman I was the result of deeply considered and precisely wrought visual imperatives, comparable to the stringent Classicism of de Kooning’s hero, J.A.D. Ingres. Hess characterizes the painting’s rapid alterations, punctuated by methodical and contemplative stopgaps, as “ambiguity exactingly sought and exactingly left undefined.”

His analysis is guided by de Kooning’s idiosyncratic process: he traces shapes and lines from the painting onto vellum at various stages so he can consult them once they’re painted out; sometimes he transfers the lifted lines onto another part of the picture, often flipped or reversed or cut up. In between de Kooning scrapes and sands down parts of the picture, “leaving hints of contradictory outline in a jewel-like haze of iridescence,” as Denby put it, while striving to maintain an all-over freshness. All this is impossible to reconstruct solely by looking at the finished painting. By contrast, the working cartoons, along with the torrent of related drawings, collages, and pastels made before, during, and after Woman I provide an archaeological record of its coming into being. They hover around it like roiling psychic weather, extending it with endless alternative solutions—sought and considered, affirmed or rejected—and presenting the artist as a thinker of almost unfathomable virtuosity and seemingly limitless experimental capability.

Advertisement

The case study of the restless interaction of hand and mind first presented in “De Kooning Paints a Picture” is expanded to encompass his entire life’s work in the Art Institute of Chicago’s exhibition “Willem de Kooning Drawing.” It’s an instructive follow-up to the Museum of Modern Art’s magisterial “de Kooning: A Retrospective” of fifteen years ago, which included around two hundred works, only about a quarter of which were on paper, thus casting them in a traditional supporting role to the cavalcade of large canvases. By contrast, the Art Institute’s exhibition presents the same number of works with the proportions reversed: almost all are modestly scaled and on some form of paper, except for seven canvases and about a dozen bronze sculptures presented within the conceptual rubric of “drawing.”

To describe these as “paper” and “canvas” rather than “drawings” and “paintings” signals the sly provocation of the exhibition. As Hess writes in his authoritative study Willem de Kooning: Drawings (1972), in which he explicates a selection of 128 graphic works:

A close examination of de Kooning’s drawings first of all tends to dissolve any possible definition of “drawing.” It is as if this master draftsman had systematically eliminated the graphic as an element that can be isolated in art. One cannot even set the drawings apart by putting them in a category of “works on paper,” for many of de Kooning’s paintings are also on paper, and what collectors take to be oils on board or on canvas are in fact papers which have been mounted after the picture was finished. This eluding of categories and definitions is a major aspect of the content of de Kooning’s art.

What comes to the fore in the early paintings Seated Man (1939) and Queen of Hearts (1943–1946) is the decisive presence of charcoal lines worked and reworked into the picture, making it a hybrid object: a drawing embedded in paint. In later “paintings,” when this kind of drawing has melted into a skin of fluidly applied brushstrokes, these marks can be read as a continuation of drawing, a touch that finds and refines itself on the surface with immediacy and intimacy.

The exhibition is organized chronologically, following de Kooning’s biography alongside the formal evolution of certain sequences and the many experiments that are the connective tissue among the major works on view. Born in Rotterdam in 1904 to working-class parents who soon split acrimoniously, as a boy he shuttled between a physically and emotionally abusive mother and an eerily remote father, both of whom remarried and started new families. At twelve he was sent to work for six days a week at a prestigious decorator’s studio, where he learned everything from trompe l’oeil effects to sign lettering to art nouveau embellishment. He displayed such aptitude and diligence that the following year his employers sent him in the evenings to the Rotterdam Academy of Fine Arts and Techniques, a rigorous training in design and fine art that continued for at least the next four or five years.

The earliest work in the exhibition, Dish with Jugs (circa 1919–1921), is the result of a yearlong assignment that produced a pristinely rendered still life, smudged and stippled so that no individual markings remain. It testifies to preternatural talent molded by classical beaux-arts training, which in combination with his commercial skills gave him a technical education far beyond that of the other artists who made up the New York School.

In 1926 the twenty-two-year-old de Kooning stowed away in the engine room of a steamer headed for the United States; his only English word was “yes.” After initially working as a house painter in the Dutch enclave in Hoboken, he moved to New York City the following year and was employed as a display designer for a shoe company while integrating himself into the artists’ community forming downtown. He then was able to paint full-time for the WPA, working on biomorphic abstract murals under the direction of Fernand Léger in 1935 and 1936. After he left the project he returned to a hand-to-mouth existence punctuated by odd jobs. Throughout the 1930s de Kooning focused on a series of carefully constructed though strangely unsettled portraits of men, under the influence of his close friends Gorky and John Graham. In 1938 he met Elaine Fried, a vivacious twenty-year-old art student from Brooklyn, whom he married five years later.

Advertisement

The first gallery of “Willem de Kooning Drawing” covers his first twenty-five years, displaying juvenilia with early flashes of brilliance—the zagging contours in an illustration of men’s suits already bear the skewed humor of his line—that lead to his mature works, in which something starts to coalesce around his explorations of the figure. Most striking, perhaps because it appears at first so unusual, is a small graphite portrait of Elaine (circa 1940–1941) made after they’d been together for a couple years but before they married. She sits in a tunic with slightly bunched drapery hiding the voluptuous body that de Kooning had begun to use as his figure model. Outlines and folds—a button on the cuff, fingernails—are depicted with utmost delicacy. But everything seems unfinished when compared to the face, where strokes utterly evaporate. No matter how closely you look at the eyelids, nostrils, or what Hess dubs the “tour-de-force rendition of the countercurves in the upper lip,” there are no lines, only a sculpted plane set back into the imaginary space of the drawing while resting on the surface of the paper.

It’s routinely described as Ingres-esque, but it has a psychological intensity unlike anything Ingres ever made. De Kooning is looking at Elaine as hard as he can, and she is looking back at him with equal vehemence, an unstoppable force confronting an immovable object. The disjunction between the face and everything else gives the image a feeling of having been fixated upon to the point of exhaustion, then suddenly abandoned. It was one of de Kooning’s last works that reached back to the immaculate academic still life, and Elaine recalled picking it up off the studio floor after he declared it the kind of drawing that “you could lose your mind doing.” Hess stresses in his commentary

that the sharp, taut, psychologically troubling quality in the drawing comes from the artist’s concentration on his chosen medium. De Kooning is not telling us an anecdote or engaging in autobiography. On the contrary; if he is obsessed, it is with the tiny motions of the pencil point.

Be that as it may, it is undeniable that whatever makes this drawing a representation of Elaine specifically—as opposed to any other young woman, fantasy or archetype—generates its almost terrifying power. Her own painted self-portraits from the mid-1940s share a strikingly similar look, produced by the artist locking eyes with herself in a mirror. And as unlikely as it might seem stylistically, this sketch prefigures Woman I: the same large eyes are blazing out of that work begun a decade later.

When pressed, de Kooning maintained that his Woman paintings “had to do with the female painted through all the ages, all those idols,” which is to say, with one of the central subjects of oil painting as it developed since the Renaissance. The assertion did nothing to stave off whatever biographical and psychoanalytic interpretations happened to be in vogue at the time: the hated mother, the overbearing wife, the classical goddess, the fertility idol. Elaine was annoyed enough by the gossip to ask Hans Namuth to photograph her in front of one of the Woman paintings, hoping to prove once and for all that it wasn’t a portrait of her. After that tongue-in-cheek gesture, she reported entering into a more complex relation to it: “I was fascinated to discover that I became part of the painting, as though I were the ‘Woman’s’ daughter and she had her hand, protectively, on my shoulder.”

How to navigate such entanglements of art and life—whether the painting invokes de Kooning’s mother or wife or Rubens’s Venus or the Venus of Willendorf, some combination of all of them, or none of them and is simply an arrangement of colored shapes—remains an insoluble question, suspended between extremes of formalist separation and illustrative reduction. That space of vertiginous contingency and mirage-like ambiguity is the true province of de Kooning’s art and can be uniquely accessed through his thousands of extant sketches, tracings, and collages.

The same year that Elaine began writing for ART news, Willem at age forty-four had his first solo exhibition, around ten teeming compositions that tremble between locking together and blowing apart, made of black and off-white enamel house paint accented with flashes of color. The brushwork combines luscious swells with tracery fine as a fencer’s point, activating not only the shapes themselves but the spaces between them, which step forward as shapes in their own right. In The Nation Clement Greenberg hailed de Kooning as “an outright ‘abstract’ painter,” purged of any “identifiable image.” Hot on the heels of Jackson Pollock’s first “drip” paintings exhibited months before, de Kooning seemed to fit a theory Greenberg was developing in response to the arrival of this new kind of painting. He deployed it to great rhetorical effect a few years later in his essay “‘American-Type’ Painting” (1955), which set the critical terms that haunted American art for the rest of the century.

According to Greenberg, for painting to be “truly alive in our time” it must undergo a trajectory of “self-purification,” shedding its inherited conventions one by one until it is a uniquely visual medium. A painting is a flat object, so to embrace this flatness the illusionistic “picture plane” of imagined depth must be pressed as close as possible to the surface until they all but merge. Because paintings are not actually people or landscapes or rooms or objects on a table, they should abandon such deceptions, allowing color, line, and shape to exist in their own elemental way. Narrative and language, the proper domain of literature and theater, ought also to be purged. Greenberg argued prophetically, almost mystically, that this was the only path forward for modern art, and he saw it as already underway in the work of a number of American painters—Pollock, Barnett Newman, Mark Rothko, and above all Clyfford Still—each of whom, with utterly individual approaches, was creating “a new kind of flatness, one that breathes and pulsates…. Broken by relatively few incidents of drawing or design, their surfaces exhale color with an enveloping effect.”

But this wasn’t how de Kooning saw his paintings at all. He insisted that “art never seems to make me peaceful or pure. I always seem to be wrapped in the melodrama of vulgarity.” At a symposium on abstraction at the Museum of Modern Art in 1951, he ridiculed such artistic ambitions. Through a sequence of interlinked parables he maintained that “abstraction” created a separation that had never existed, with something called “form” on the one hand and “subject matter” on the other. This false division could only cut off art from its vital connections to the larger universe of our experience. He imagined a painting that had started as a still life being labeled “abstraction”:

Until then, Art meant everything that was in it—not what you could take out of it. There was only one thing you could take out of it sometime when you were in the right mood—that abstract and identifiable sensation, the esthetic part—and still leave it where it was. For the painter to come to the “abstract” or the “nothing” he needed many things. Those things were always things in life—a horse, a flower, a milkmaid, the light in a room through a window made of diamond shapes maybe, tables, chairs, and so forth…. At that time, they were not abstract about something which was already abstract. They freed the shapes, the light, the color, the space, by putting them into concrete things in a given situation.

With a linguistic pirouette he reversed the terms: letting the color and shape also be a flower freed it. Now that liberation was being threatened: “You could not paint a house or a tree or a mountain. It was then that subject matter came into existence as something you ought not to have.” For de Kooning these prohibitions were almost literally dehumanizing. He parodied the panel’s topic with a tautology: “If I do paint abstract art, that’s what abstract art means to me. I frankly do not understand the question.”

At that time, the work de Kooning had shown publicly was plausibly en route to Greenberg’s nonrepresentational ideal, but in his studio he was already struggling with his Woman series, an interrogation of the figure in space that he’d never abandoned. The difficulty of expanding a formal language to retain both image and abstraction, depth and flatness, can be tracked by the works on paper as he tirelessly abstracts shapes from images, cycling through minor and major modifications until they are not rid of their pictorial references but seem to accrue ever more.

In the exhibition this process is demonstrated in each gallery, but nowhere more clearly than in the one devoted to the black and white enamel permutations leading into and out of his masterpiece Excavation (1950). Using black Sapolin enamel on repurposed nonabsorptive chart paper (varying between the gridded front and blank back), he laid down an incisive edge with a sign painter’s liner brush, a tool that became almost synonymous with de Kooning. The wet paint was then expertly smeared with a knife away from the line in curved solid shapes, like a shark’s fin. Rapid slashes flicker in and out of recognition: aspects of mountains and highways, windows and architecture, breasts and wheels, the propulsive movement underscored by titles like Itinerant Chapel (1951; see illustration below) and Florida Trailer (1950–1951). In them a shape is made abstract by layering pictorial possibilities rather than stripping them away, so that a single curve can evoke a handful of simultaneous associations tied to specific images and experiences—a hill, a hip—all while maintaining its identity as a line within an overall “abstract” composition.

In the second half of the 1950s and early 1960s de Kooning produced his “heroic” gestural paintings, which became his most influential abstractions: surging all-over compositions that synthesized the light and atmosphere of urban, suburban, and pastoral landscapes, notably those along the highways out to Long Island, where he relocated in 1963. For the rest of his life he pursued this intersection of line, shape, color, and texture, conjuring the optical effect of sunlight on water and sand, melding an often eroticized figure with the surrounding spaces both interior and exterior. The rest of the exhibition dramatizes his ingenious material exploration: mixing pumice with ink to create a mineralized darkness, incorporating additives to create his foamy, fatty oils, warping fixatives by rubbing and erasing to turn lines into faceted planes, and smudging pastels into inexplicable colored mists caught within hazy charcoal armatures.

From one work to the next you see de Kooning pushing his materials and abilities to the limit to learn what else they might do just on the edge of his control. There is the infamous group of drawings from the mid-1960s made with his left hand, or while watching television, or with his eyes closed. (He also molded his sketch-like clay sculptures with his eyes closed, working from touch and memory.) Out of this flurried stream-of-consciousness tumble many of his recurrent motifs but also an unexpected number of crucifixions, bodies stretched on an axis but at a receding angle, like a Rubens altarpiece. Christ on the Cross, like the figure of a woman, is another central subject of painting history, and a surprisingly direct restatement of de Kooning’s lifelong analysis of intersecting organic and geometric lines: the human body fitted within baroque space.

By the end of the 1970s his increasingly dramatic alcoholism became a serious problem, and after being estranged for some two decades, Elaine reentered his domestic life, stabilizing it enough for him to make an astonishing final body of work. Once he was sober in the early 1980s, the paintings began to thin and the compositions to simplify. His earlier drawings were used as scaffolding, transferred to the ground and then painted in sparse complex contours with gently modulated open areas between them, as though suspended in a luminous expanse. One of these untitled canvases from 1985 included in the Chicago exhibition shows a handful of cobalt and black waves and curves that intersect and overlap, like airy distended hieroglyphs. The cold white ground is tenderly amended: lines have been shortened or removed by whiting them out, which leaves a fluttering trace of their having been contemplated and reconsidered; the process, as ever, remains in the fore, visually available and ultimately inexplicable. Outside the studio the artist was exhibiting a dementia-like cognitive decline, which long led many critics to cast aspersions on these works, but their sheer visual intelligence and drop-dead elegance refute any supposed diminishment. If anything, as one of the ultimate examples of “late style,” they are achingly affecting, refined to grace alone.

De Kooning always had a unique relationship with language, as though words were simply another of his artistic materials. Many of his quotations are repeated as truisms to this day: “flesh was the reason oil paint was invented”; “even abstract shapes must have a likeness”; “content…is a glimpse of something, an encounter…like a flash.” Much has been made of the alphabetic letters in some paintings, though letters are simply a subcategory of shape, and of the fluent calligraphy of his brush, though handwriting is merely a subcategory of line. Like de Kooning’s conception of images and art history, both are aimed at expanding the semantic scope of painterly language.

His titles, sometimes suggested by friends, are so consistently evocative that they could only have been chosen by him: Door to the River, Easter Monday, Rosy-Fingered Dawn at Louse Point. But more fundamentally, in de Kooning there is an unusual awareness of language as integral to visual form itself. He told the critic David Sylvester in 1960: “The very fact that [Woman I] had a word connected with it—‘figure of a woman’—made it more precise. Perhaps I am more of a novelist than a poet…but I always like the word in painting.”

As Hess described first in “Paints a Picture” and as the entire “Willem de Kooning Drawing” exhibition demonstrates, de Kooning’s process was profoundly dialogic, the painter confronting and confronted by an open field: a mark would be made, then studied at length, a visual call and response by which the painting was constructed through a process of looking and thinking that could not be premeditated or circumvented and that was carried on from one work to the next. This conception still, even unconsciously, undergirds what is meant by “painting” in New York City to this day. In 1981 he described his process as a form of talking: “When the thing starts to talk to me, I know what to do. I’m not always right but I think I know what to do.”

De Kooning’s three published major statements—two lectures transcribed and edited by Elaine and the other excised from a conversation with Sylvester and reconstructed as a monologue—can be understood as extensions of dialogue. They fit comfortably among the many other interviews in which you hear de Kooning’s quickening mind, how he thrives on the unexpected back and forth. As in the action of the drawings, you get the sense of how funny he is. Take the deadpan delivery in Emile de Antonio’s documentary Painters Painting (1972) when de Kooning announces, “I don’t think painters have particularly bright ideas.” The filmmaker asks what they have instead. “I guess their talent is painting things. It’s not such a bright idea for Monet to paint those haystacks, different hours of the day.” A smile grows as he says it, and then he breaks into laughter.

In de Kooning’s stories there are many similarly unexpected reversals, as in the opening salvo of his 1951 discussion of abstraction at MoMA:

The first man who began to speak, whoever he was, must have intended it. For surely it is talking that has put “Art” into painting. Nothing is positive about art except that it is a word. Right from there to here all art became literary. We are not yet living in a world where everything is self-evident. It is very interesting to notice that a lot of people who want to take the talking out of painting, for instance, do nothing else but talk about it. That is not contradiction, however. The art in it is the forever mute part you can talk about forever.

When words like “abstract” or “pure” are put in proximity to paintings, they change how we see them. They are the vehicle by which a formal element becomes recognizable and then legible, and that we can go on talking about it makes it meaningful. Without this atmosphere of talk, there is no art worth having, just as without the specificity of “a horse, a flower, a milkmaid, the light in a room,” there is nothing but circles and squares. Of course pictures depicting people and nameable things can be just as meaningless, as the deluge of contemporary figurative painting has made obvious. If many of today’s formally anemic paintings can be dismissed as “illustrative” or “academic,” this is largely enabled by the language now used to discuss them, which does not rise above description of the subject matter. Something rarely said alongside the continual declaration of a “crisis of criticism” is that it is also a “crisis of art.”

Today’s histrionics around artificial intelligence throw into relief a definition of art so obvious that it remains largely unarticulated: something made by human beings for other human beings to think about, primarily through looking. Such a definition brings back uncomfortable and long-discredited mythologies of the artist, especially those who embody virtuosity as de Kooning does. However, if we accept that art is an inherently human endeavor, then there is no clean way to sever the purely visual experience of an individual painting from everything else humans do—our relationships with friends and lovers, with paintings and books from throughout history, with highways and beaches. The way these stories are threaded through the artworks makes them more interesting, sometimes sadder, more disturbing, or more beautiful than pigment on canvas or paper could otherwise be. All of this is right there on the surface, but it also extends invisibly all around, between people and across time; it is the forever mute part we will talk about forever.
