entries.content:
My father brought books to the basement.

During the air raids we read

Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea, Treasure Island,

Around the World in Eighty Days,

and ate feasts my mother made with dry goods and powdered milk:

rice pudding, “béchamel” spaghetti,

in one large aluminum pot over a small gas burner,

sandwiches of Picon cheese

she cut in triangles, like a tea party.

We had tea party

picnics

in the basement

or on the small patch of green

by the road.

And after reading Aladdin, I spent a day sitting

on the carpet in the living room

cross-legged, clutching the edges and hoping.

entries.title: Sad-Maxxing
entries.summary: Ashton Politanoff's new novel tells the story of sad dads and washed-up jocks vying for a phantom ideal of masculinity.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In her 2018 memoir You All Grow Up and Leave Me, the journalist Piper Weiss recalls her teenage years as a tennis player under the guidance of Gary Wilensky, who ran his own coaching company, Gary’s Girls and Guys Adult and Junior Tennis Programs, in New York City during the 1990s. Wilensky was not a professional tennis player, and he wasn’t even that talented on the court. What he did have, as Weiss explains, was “a natural ability to read people, easily detecting their strengths and weaknesses.” He also made tennis fun. Other coaches might bully or belittle young players, but Wilensky presented himself as “an entertainer, a clown with a sack full of gags, doling out carnival prizes on the courts, and showing up for lessons in the occasional costume.” At some point the Eastern Tennis Association named him coach of the year.

Like Weiss, I took lessons through Gary’s Girls and Guys, for several months starting when I was eight years old. Wilensky was never my teacher, but he was always around—a rumpled figure with an air of passive benevolence. He was also head coach for the tennis team at my all-girls private school, and I would often see him in the lobby, decked out in a polyester tracksuit that rustled as he walked. In late April 1993, as I sat at the kitchen table watching the evening news, I saw Wilensky’s name on the screen. He was dead of a self-inflicted gunshot wound, just hours after trying and failing to kidnap one of his seventeen-year-old students. The police found a cabin Wilensky had rented in the Adirondacks, which New York magazine dubbed a “House of Horrors.” It was full of “sadomasochistic paraphernalia”: chains, handcuffs, a mask, a rubber sex doll.

Despite “all the diagnoses used to explain Gary’s mind-set,” Weiss writes, it is the doll that provides “the most visceral indication of what gripped him in his final days: his disconnect from real relationships, the conflicts of his desire, and his delusional belief that a young woman was an object he could fold up and store away.” This is a thoughtful way of saying that Wilensky was a loser. Adrift in the adult world, he played the champion with children and built a fantasy life premised on the illusion of his own competence. Grown-up intimacy was impossible: he had been married for six months in the late 1960s but divorced, according to his father, Irving, to focus on tennis, which Irving had taught him to play at the age of five. “He was one a father could be proud of,” Irving told reporters after Gary’s death. “He did not seem like the kind of guy who would do something like this.”

What kinds of guys are there? This is one of the questions posed by Ashton Politanoff’s acrid and exceptionally readable second novel, Dad Had a Bad Day, which follows a middle-aged man as he tries to recapture his glory days as an up-and-coming teenage tennis player, with results that are at first mixed and finally devastating. Feeling emasculated by unemployment—his wife, who travels often for work but whose occupation is never specified, makes just enough to keep the household afloat—and by serving as the primary caregiver to his six-year-old son, Ned Lafferty impulsively joins the local country club, using a credit card to pay for membership along with a new racket and a pharmacopoeia of protein powders and other elixirs of youth. He is drawn to the men he sees at the club, “a new species” driven by “ritual, discipline, and refinement,” with “good habits” he hopes will “rub off” on him. Soon he is captain of the club’s men’s team, jockeying for supremacy against other husbands and fathers who seem, contrary to Ned’s veneration of them, just as lonely and disaffected as he is, or else becoming sick with envy of the younger, more athletic patrons who have yet to begin the long slide into midlife crisis.

Here are sad dads and washed-up jocks, suburbanites in their thirties and forties dipping their toes into the manosphere by embracing its protocols of relentless self-optimization (also known as “maxxing”). They lift weights, chug shakes, and play tennis until they puke, then drink too many beers at the club’s restaurant. Many of them, including Ned and his childhood friend and rival, Roland, are scarred by their time as youth players, haunted by memories of the sadistic coaches and cruel, competitive fathers who terrorized them both on and off the court. Masculinity, in this novel, is an inheritance of anguish and misadventure—one battle after another in which boy is pitted against boy and then man against man, all of them vying for a phantom ideal of total immunity from the frustrations and injustices of ordinary life.

Advertisement

Amateur competitive tennis makes a good backdrop for all this testosterone-fueled flailing. Tennis is traditionally a rich person’s game, with a higher outlay than the great populist pastimes of soccer and basketball. It is also home to the infamously explosive temperaments of John McEnroe and Jimmy Connors and to the unapologetic sexism and racism directed at stars from Billie Jean King to the Williams sisters to Naomi Osaka. (In 2016 computer scientists at Cornell University published a study showing that journalists are exponentially more likely to ask female tennis players questions that are unrelated to the sport, such as where they like to shop or, as one inquired of Serena Williams in 2015, why they don’t smile more.) In other words, tennis is something of a whited sepulcher, its genteel façade concealing considerable rot.

“The game of tennis,” according to Politanoff’s epigraph, “was originally played by monks.” The game, in this case, was probably jeu de paume, which dates back to twelfth-century France. It involves smacking a ball with your bare hand instead of a racket and does indeed seem to have been played in monasteries. As for rackets, they were added a few centuries later. In his Troilus and Criseyde, completed sometime in the 1380s, Chaucer has Troilus upbraid his friend Pandare by comparing him to a “raket” that plays “to and fro,/Nettle in, dok out, now this, now that.” Better known is a scene from the first act of Shakespeare’s Henry V, in which a French ambassador presents King Henry with a gift of tennis balls from the Dauphin—a cheeky allusion to the erstwhile Prince Hal’s misspent youth. Henry is unamused. “When we have matched our rackets to these balls,” he warns, “we will in France, by God’s grace, play a set/Shall strike” the French king’s “crown into the hazard.”

In the mid-sixteenth century, a younger brother of the great essayist Michel de Montaigne died after a tennis ball hit him in the head. Caravaggio is said to have killed a man over a tennis match, although his biographer Andrew Graham-Dixon thinks it more likely that he killed a man in a duel on a tennis court. Variants of the sport remained enormously popular throughout the Renaissance—Anne Boleyn was watching a game at Hampton Court Palace when she was arrested—but its popularity declined in the eighteenth century, when cards and billiards replaced it as the aristocrat’s diversion of choice. It does make a cameo, however, in one of the most important events leading up to the French Revolution. On June 20, 1789, members of France’s Third Estate met on an indoor tennis court at Versailles and swore not to dissolve until they had written their country a new constitution. This is known as the Tennis Court Oath.

No one had much time for tennis in revolutionary France, but the sport thrived in England, where the first Wimbledon was held in 1877. Just four years later, the first US National Championship, now called the US Open, was held on grass courts at Newport Casino in Rhode Island. But tennis became newly trendy in the 1970s and 1980s, when televised matches made celebrities out of players like McEnroe, a brilliant tactician and hothead who earned himself the nickname SuperBrat, the power forehand pioneer Boris “Boom Boom” Becker, tough-as-nails Martina Navratilova (“the Iron Lady”), and Navratilova’s unflappable rival, Chris Evert (“the Ice Maiden”). The sport entered a new phase with the rise of Venus and Serena Williams, who, in the 1990s, brought a much-needed diversity to a mostly lily-white milieu.

In 2025 tennis was the fourth-most-popular sport in the world. For six consecutive years it added new players, its growth led by women and people under thirty-five. The game holds special appeal in a culture obsessed with finding new bulwarks against aging. The Copenhagen City Heart Study, an ongoing epidemiological research project begun in 1976, has found that recreational tennis players live on average 9.7 years longer than people who don’t regularly exercise—much better results than swimming (3.4 years), cycling (3.7 years), or jogging (3.2 years). Mark Kovacs, a coach and physiologist, told The New York Times earlier this year that the benefits are as much mental as they are cardiovascular. “Cognitively demanding and intrinsically social,” tennis forces us to react in real time to another person. Moreover, it is best played not in a cortisol-spiking frenzy but with titrated sangfroid. As W. Timothy Gallwey put it in his beloved self-help manual The Inner Game of Tennis, first published in 1974, “The secret to winning any game lies in not trying too hard.”

Alas for Ned Lafferty. When we meet him, he is thirty-nine and already in the midst of a fast-moving nervous breakdown. He’s been laid off from his job, and he and his wife have struck a bargain that will be familiar to many a single-income household: since he’s not working, “Daddy daycare it is.” In the novel’s first pages, Ned is stuck at home with his son, Freddie, who is out sick from school. For no apparent reason, he walks into the garage and digs out his old racket, swinging it back and forth. The next thing we know, he is touring the Wind and Sea Tennis Club and enrolling Freddie in the club’s on-site childcare. Bribing him with toys from Target, Ned extracts from Freddie a promise not to tell his mother, a secret that will become increasingly difficult to keep after Ned—a former champion who’s “tasted glory” on the court—gets himself hired as the captain of the men’s summer tennis team and begins spending every waking hour at the Wind and Sea. Sometimes he sneaks off while his son is asleep. In one harrowing scene, he leaves Freddie at a stranger’s birthday party in a public park so he can go practice with his team.

Advertisement

Narrating the book in a hollowed-out, vaguely menacing first person, Ned shuttles between the present, in which he may be losing his mind, and the past, where the seeds of his current dysfunction are sown. “Every week they ask you,” he says of his life as an eleven-year-old player, “What’s your rank? How’d you do? What round did you get to?” But they never ask, “Did you have fun?” His alcoholic stepfather wouldn’t speak to him “for days” if he lost a match, even as “he would tell everyone he knew, including members of the club, my coaches, that I had won the whole tournament.” In college his coach makes him throw tennis balls across the court until he injures himself badly. Ned’s response to this setback brings about the end of his tennis career, until he resurfaces at the Wind and Sea.

Politanoff himself was once a Division I tennis player, and his terse, ominous prose is stippled with technical terms and sports slang, whizzing by like so many Dunlop ATPs. Players will hit “a slice, a drive, a heavy ball, a drop shot” or “a nice ice-cream floater.” His unnumbered chapters are short, but a lot happens in each one—not unlike, you might say, a tennis match, where the governing tension between a compact field of play and balls that can reach speeds of more than 150 miles per hour creates an environment at once tightly contained and incredibly volatile. In the space of a few paragraphs, Ned will abandon and recover his child, bungle an extramarital affair, win and lose, experience ecstasy and dejection. He is high on his own poor choices, which, for all their stupidity, seem to bring a much-needed urgency to his disappointed life.

Several reviews of Dad Had a Bad Day have focused on the story’s relationship to toxic masculinity. The term, which has become ubiquitous, is often attributed to the psychologist Shepherd Bliss, though its exact provenance is unclear. In 2019 Bliss defined it simply as behavior by men “that diminishes women, children, [and] other men.” Today the phrase describes everything from the crimes of Andrew and Tristan Tate—social media stars who promote misogyny along with intermittent fasting and who were arrested in July 2026 on charges of rape and sex trafficking—to the stern injunction to kids that boys don’t cry. Last year the British television series Adolescence was widely lauded for its exploration of the phenomenon among schoolchildren, and in particular of the Internet-based subcultures that promote hateful attitudes toward women while encouraging boys to cultivate a persona that combines the irrepressible id of a caveman, the grandiosity of a mob boss, and the jet-setting avarice of Jordan Belfort, the fraudulent stockbroker immortalized in Martin Scorsese’s 2013 film The Wolf of Wall Street.*

In a recent interview in the Los Angeles Review of Books, Politanoff acknowledged that Ned’s attempts to make himself fitter, hotter, more attractive to women and more intimidating to men are “totally playing off” toxic masculinists like “Ben Greenfield, Joe Rogan, Paul Chek, and all these names that became relevant during the Covid-19 lockdown for their self-improvement hacks, life hacks, biohacks.” “I hired a personal trainer named Mason,” Ned reports. “We focused on the main muscle groups—back, chest, shoulders, biceps, triceps, quads, hamstrings, glutes, calves.” He also hires “a tennis coach named Joachim,” whom he describes as “a Norwegian-Swede mix,” and a masseuse named Vasanta. Meanwhile,

I made smoothies at home with power greens, pitted dates, blueberries, almond milk, vanilla-flavored plant-based protein powder, and cacao nibs. I purchased some polos, some grommets, some string savers, head and lead tape, athletic boxer briefs, jock-itch cream, moisture-control sports socks, antifungal foot spray, callus and corn shaver, some tea-tree foot scrub. I purchased books with titles such as Champion Mindset and Mental Toughness in Tennis. I applied zinc oxide to the bridge of my nose. I stood in front of the mirror and repeated positive affirmations. I kept a journal. I charged everything to the secret credit card I kept behind my driver’s license in my Montblanc wallet.

Here is the vocabulary, and the shopping list, of the manosphere, right down to that crypto-eugenicist detail about the ethnicity of Ned’s coach. That detail chimes with an earlier moment in the novel, when Ned ruefully compares his own “swarthy” features with his wife’s and son’s blond hair, light eyes, and fair skin. There is, as Politanoff says, “a lot of humor” to be found here but also a lot of menace. Like Greenfield et al., Ned aspires to be an Übermensch: a superior human specimen whose body has been engineered for excellence, supercharged by nut milks and purged of undesirable elements, from foot fungus to negative thoughts. It is an identity in conflict with his role as a twenty-first-century parent, which requires him to be a gentle, endlessly patient caretaker who apologizes when he yells and stays in the bathroom with Freddie while the boy shits—a “mother bird,” as Ned puts it, instead of an alpha male.

There is no question that disagreeable, even dangerous attitudes toward masculinity play a significant part in Politanoff’s novel, which is propelled by Ned’s realization that he can no longer bear being a stay-at-home dad in a sexless marriage. But in its preoccupation with what Politanoff calls the “abject-adjacent features” of manospheric culture, Dad Had a Bad Day also has something in common with Ottessa Moshfegh’s My Year of Rest and Relaxation (2018) and Yasmin Zaher’s The Coin (2024), books that similarly test the boundary between self-care and self-destruction. In The Coin, a young woman with a taste for Birkin bags and luxury skin care shaves and scrubs every plane of her body until her bathtub is filled with hair, dead skin, and fingernail clippings. In My Year of Rest and Relaxation, another young woman uses psychiatric drugs to force herself into a part-time coma. She calls it “hibernating” and spends her days and nights either asleep or watching movies. “I stopped tweezing,” she says, “stopped bleaching, stopped waxing, stopped brushing my hair. No moisturizing or exfoliating. No shaving.”

While these earlier novels are obviously interested in the drama of feminine upkeep, with its strange commixture of decadence and asceticism, it would be wrong to reduce them to meditations on gender. Zaher’s heroine, like the novelist herself, is Palestinian, and The Coin proposes an oblique but unmistakable link between her obsession with cleanliness and the killing fields of her homeland. Looking down at that bathtub, she sees “thin long hairs like supple grass, clusters of pubic hair like spindly bushes,” the “primordial matter” of slimy soap “pooling around the dead bodies” of her skin and nails, “cuticles in rows like limestone terraces.” “It was beautiful,” she concludes, “like summer in Palestine.” Agonizingly unsentimental, My Year of Rest and Relaxation—which is, for the most part, set in a pre–September 11 New York City full of vacuous party people, frat-boy bankers, and art-world vultures—is emptied of anything that might make existence seem worthwhile. And yet Moshfegh’s protagonist seems to believe that death is more than life deserves. She opts for inertia over suicide, allowing her body’s slow deterioration to stand as an indictment of a world she never fully leaves behind.

Similarly, Ned’s manic ablutions have a despairing quality that suggests masochism as much as a desire to excel. He drinks beer in an ice bath that feels “like a thousand tiny needles stabbing” him at once. He makes himself two batches of Sumatran coffee—first in a French press and then with a Chemex, “using a brown filter, unbleached”—and then continues his morning routine:

I toasted the heel piece of cracked sourdough and ate it without butter. I had to go to the bathroom frequently. I did some pushups on the hardwood to ground myself…. I put on some sunscreen. I watched the highlights from Halle, a warm-up grass-court tournament before Wimbledon. I ate a protein bar. I made myself a smoothie with dried mango, arugula, peanut butter, ice, and 2%. I poured it into the sink after one sip. I messaged my squad: Match still on for noon, courts should be dry. I tied the end of a red band around the sliding door handle like a tourniquet and proceeded to tug it in various ways as part of my rotator cuff exercise regimen.

There is little pleasure to be found here. Ned’s meals, such as they are, are tasteless and punishing, sending him running to the toilet between rounds of push-ups. As for exercise, it suggests only injury, that tourniquet calling up images of soldiers bleeding out on a battlefield. The whole passage swells with small but telling signifiers of bourgeois comfort—the pricey food items, the hardwood floors, the studied attention to one’s own body (putting on sunscreen, having a “regimen”)—that feel strangely uncomfortable, as if Ned were in a torture chamber rather than a nice suburban home. Part of our unease comes from knowing that he is living beyond his means, and that his bubble is surely going to burst. But we are also repelled because Ned’s environment is itself repulsive, empty of beauty or meaning and representing nothing except the money that furnishes it.

For all that it satirizes male delusion and middle-class ennui, Dad Had a Bad Day stops short of political critique, which allows it to maintain its light touch. There are moments, however, when it seems to point toward a better life than the one Ned feverishly pursues, riven as it is by competition over women, resources, and self-respect. Some of these moments involve Ned’s imperfect yet still undeniably loving rapport with his son. Others foreground his tenderness toward other men. Ned calls this tenderness “a kinship,” but occasionally it seems like erotic interest. After he showers next to a young man at the club, he takes some time to look at his body:

He was backlit by a small window and naked, with one leg up on the marble counter, his balls and penis dangling. He was using a boar bristled hairbrush on his leg, starting from up high, on the inside. His leg hair was curled and finally groomed—it looked like bronze fleece.

Another time, Ned watches a man “with no pubic hair” rub lotion into his belly “like he was massaging dough.” When he plays with his old friend Roland, he notices that Roland hits “a hard, penetrating ball concealed by relaxed strokes and minimal movement”—a description that might be applied, under different circumstances, to a good lover.

These sensual glimmers are no match for the antagonistic sociality of straight male relationships, which, in this novel, quickly convert sympathy or desire into rivalry and aggression. Inevitably, the camaraderie between Ned and his teammates will sour, sometimes turning violent; just as inevitably, his secret hobby will be discovered, his marriage imperiled, his delusions exposed. All the same, his carnal curiosity about other men feels far more urgent than his frustrated longing for his wife, who brushes off his advances and masturbates in the shower, or the female club member with whom he almost has an affair. Other than Ned’s love for his son, it is the only thing in his world that isn’t ugly—or expensive. Perhaps in another lifetime, or another novel, Ned would find a way to nourish these intimations of benevolence or even love, refusing to let them be spoiled by his own aspirational machismo. Unfortunately, he is not that kind of guy.

  • *

    See Hari Kunzru, “Surviving the Manosphere,” The New York Review, October 9, 2025.

entries.content:
Ever since the end of the cold war, the subject of nuclear war and the profound threat it poses to humanity has suffered a “peculiar invisibility.” This is the phrase the German philosopher Günther Anders used in his book The Obsolescence of the Human (1956) to illuminate the roots of the “Apokalypse-Blindheit”—“apocalypse blindness”—that had begun to set in just a few years after the dropping of atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.1 Seventy years on, despite the construction of gigantic nuclear arsenals and several near catastrophes, the blindness persists.

Today each of America’s fourteen nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines is capable of launching 160 warheads with a combined explosive force of up to 73,000 kilotons, roughly the equivalent of five thousand Hiroshimas. The Russians possess a similar capability. A mere fraction of the nuclear weapons that exist today could kill millions of people within minutes. Hundreds of detonations could ignite massive fires, lofting soot into the atmosphere and blocking sunlight, potentially triggering a nuclear winter. The resulting disruption to global food systems would threaten billions of people with starvation.

This dark reality is so apocalyptic that most people just ignore it. Public opinion surveys consistently show that while many say nuclear weapons are a danger, they don’t rank them as a major concern. Nuclear issues are nowhere to be found in Gallup’s polling of the most important problems facing the country. Those in authority rarely talk about nuclear war. The news media rarely mention it. Attention to the issue has been confined to a cadre of professionals—government officials, college professors, think tank specialists, and nuclear lab employees—who think, write, and talk in such abstract language that the horrors of nuclear destruction are obscured or minimized.

The danger not only remains, it is increasing. Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump—whose countries together hold nearly 90 percent of global nuclear stockpiles—wake up every morning with the authority to wipe out entire cities. The United States has embarked on a trillion-dollar modernization of its aging nuclear arsenal; Russia is replacing all its Soviet-era nuclear systems and adding new ones. The theory—really a kind of belief system—underpinning this buildup is known as “nuclear deterrence.” It dictates that each country threatens the other with annihilation, thereby instilling such fear that neither uses the awful power they possess.

The horrible precariousness of this situation is compounded by the fact that over the past twenty-five years, with barely a political ripple, the treaties limiting the size and deployment of the US and Russian nuclear arsenals have lapsed or been abandoned. This began in 2002, when President George W. Bush, influenced by advocates for a nationwide missile defense system, pulled out of the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty, signed in 1972. It continued in 2019, when Trump withdrew the US from the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty of 1987, which had eliminated an entire class of nuclear weapons, and this year, again under Trump, with the expiration of the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, which since 2011 had provided for on-site inspections and limited the number of US and Russian nuclear warheads and missiles.

Now there is nothing to restrain the US or Russia other than Trump’s or Putin’s personal assessment of national interest. China, meanwhile, has been accelerating its nuclear buildup. And nuclear war planners rely more and more on artificial intelligence, which automates the process and reduces the time for human judgment.

In 1945 a group of scientists who worked on the Manhattan Project created the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists. Two years later they established the Doomsday Clock, which rates the world’s vulnerability to human-caused global catastrophe. The Bulletin uses the imagery of nuclear apocalypse—a countdown to midnight—to convey threats to humanity. This year the Bulletin’s Science and Security Board, in consultation with its Board of Sponsors—which Albert Einstein and J. Robert Oppenheimer helped create—set the clock at eighty-five seconds to midnight. This is the closest it has ever been.

Three recent books attempt to explain how we got into this mess. In The Nuclear Age, Serhii Plokhy, a historian at Harvard, provides a sweeping account of the science, politics, and history of nuclear technology. He begins with H.G. Wells, who coined the term “atomic bomb” in his novel The World Set Free (1914). Wells’s vision of a new weapon of immense power began to seem plausible in the 1930s, as scientists in different countries discovered that bombarding uranium with neutrons could produce a chain reaction—nuclear fission. In August 1939 Einstein and other prominent physicists signed a letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt urging him to build an atomic bomb before the Germans did, which led to the Manhattan Project.

Oppenheimer directed the laboratory at Los Alamos, New Mexico, that designed the first atomic bombs. In 1946 he drafted a report that recommended the creation of an international authority to own and control all fissile and nuclear materials. Bernard Baruch, the US representative to the newly established United Nations Atomic Energy Commission, incorporated these ideas into a plan that he presented that same year at the UN. Among its provisions was a stipulation that the permanent members of the UN Security Council would not have veto power over decisions to punish nuclear violations. Joseph Stalin refused to agree to this. The Soviet Union countered with a demand that the US destroy its nuclear weapons before any international authority was created, but the distrust between the two countries made that impossible. The Soviet Union tested its own nuclear weapon in 1949, and other countries followed.

Advertisement

After Stalin died in 1953, relations between the US and the Soviet Union began to improve. In 1959 Nikita Khrushchev visited America, and talks were planned for a summit in Paris the following year. But just as the meeting was about to begin the Soviets shot down an American U-2 spy plane that had been surveilling Soviet missile capacity. Khrushchev was outraged and asked President Dwight D. Eisenhower to apologize. When he didn’t, Khrushchev broke up the summit—and so began decades of missed opportunities.

In 1960 John F. Kennedy was elected president after a campaign in which he asserted that the US was falling behind the Soviet Union in the nuclear arms race—the so-called missile gap—though he knew that U-2 surveillance had shown this to be false. Both Kennedy and Eisenhower approved the stationing of nuclear missiles in Turkey, though they privately expressed doubts about doing so. In response Khrushchev put Soviet missiles in Cuba, which resulted in the Cuban missile crisis. That near catastrophe led to the signing of the first formal nuclear arms treaty between the US and the Soviet Union in 1963, which banned above-ground and underwater testing of nuclear weapons. This inaugurated a series of arms agreements but did not prevent either country from building tens of thousands more.

Despite the Vietnam War, relations between the US and the USSR improved sufficiently for Richard Nixon and Leonid Brezhnev to bring about a period of détente in the late 1960s and early 1970s. During this period American and Soviet negotiators conducted the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks (SALT I), which led to an interim agreement and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty. These agreements imposed some limits on nuclear weapons and banned most antiballistic missile defense systems. The Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty was remarkable in that it led both countries to accept their vulnerability.

The good feeling didn’t last long. In 1974 President Gerald Ford signed the Vladivostok Accord, paving the way for SALT II. Facing mounting criticism for being too soft on the Soviets, as well as competition from Ronald Reagan in his 1976 reelection bid, Ford appointed an outside group of hawkish experts to evaluate the CIA’s estimate of Soviet offensive capacity. Known as Team B, they delivered a report that emphasized hostile Soviet intentions and missile strength. It was later revealed to be grossly exaggerated, yet it was so alarming that the subsequent Carter administration launched a nuclear buildup, which accelerated in the 1980s under Reagan.2

Plokhy takes this story up to 2024 and the current war in Ukraine, in which Russia has targeted several nuclear power plants. He warns that the world’s approximately 440 nuclear power plants are now likely military targets. We are, he concludes, in “a more dangerous situation today than we have been since the Cuban missile crisis of 1962.”

In Nuclear Weapons: An International History, David Holloway, a historian at Stanford, uses diaries and other previously confidential records to tell a chilling story of how the leaders of countries with nuclear weapons perceived—and misperceived—one another in the latter half of the twentieth century. The Soviet Union and the US both believed that the other was determined to strike first.3 Each genuinely feared the other and recognized the horrors that a nuclear war would bring, yet that did not stop them from taking perilous risks on many occasions. “Neither Truman nor Stalin,” Holloway writes, “saw the bomb solely or even primarily as a common danger to be addressed by cooperative action.” That is a sentiment apparently shared today by Trump, Putin, and Xi Jinping.

Distrust and competition were present from the technology’s earliest days. Holloway recounts how the Danish physicist Niels Bohr, who visited the Manhattan Project, did his best to convince both Winston Churchill and Roosevelt to raise with Stalin the question of how to manage the unprecedented power of atomic energy. He foresaw the “fateful competition” that would result from keeping Stalin in the dark about the atomic bomb that America was getting ready to use on Japan. Bohr failed in this effort. Two weeks after the US bombing of Hiroshima, Stalin gave the order to create a Soviet bomb, an enormous scientific and industrial undertaking that involved hundreds of thousands of workers. The Soviet Union tested an atomic bomb on August 29, 1949. Less than two months later, President Harry S. Truman approved a request from the Joint Chiefs of Staff to increase the US nuclear stockpile—an endless cycle of action and reaction.

Advertisement

Instead of the proposed international body to control nuclear weapons technology, the deeply flawed concept of deterrence emerged. In 1946 the American military strategist Bernard Brodie gave the classic formulation: the US had to possess “in case of attack the possibility of retaliation in kind,” which meant by the end of the Eisenhower administration the ability to launch enough nuclear weapons to kill 600 million people. “Thus far the chief purpose of our military establishment has been to win wars,” Brodie wrote. “From now on its chief purpose must be to avert them.”

In January 1950, five months after the Soviets tested their first atomic bomb, Truman announced the development of the significantly more powerful hydrogen bomb. Three months later his national security staff produced a secret policy paper known as NSC-68, which described the Soviets as “animated by a new fanatic faith” and called for an enormous military buildup of conventional and nuclear forces to counter an implacable and expansionary foe. Together with the Korean War, this led to a huge increase in the US defense budget. In October 1950 Truman authorized a multibillion-dollar “expansion program” that bolstered or added nuclear facilities in Oak Ridge, Hanford, Savannah River, and several other places, with a total cost exceeding that of the Manhattan Project. Then, in January 1952, he approved a longer-term program to further expand US nuclear capacity to match an expected Soviet buildup. The Defense Department argued that the US needed a “greater advantage” over the Soviets, which Stalin was never going to accept—a formula for endless, futile escalation.

In 1962, when Kennedy found out that Khrushchev had stationed nuclear missiles in Cuba, he demanded that they be removed. Though the Joint Chiefs recommended an air strike to destroy the missiles, with an invasion of Cuba to follow, Kennedy imposed a naval quarantine instead. If he had chosen to invade, it seems likely that other nuclear weapons on the island—unknown to the US—would have been launched, causing devastating American casualties. Thirty years later, Robert McNamara, Kennedy’s secretary of defense, described the event as “horrifying…. There was a 99 percent probability that nuclear war would have been initiated.”

After Kennedy agreed not to invade Cuba and—secretly—to pull US missiles out of Turkey, Khrushchev removed the Cuban missiles, and the US and the Soviet Union set up a hotline for direct communication. But there immediately followed a huge buildup of nuclear weapons by both countries, which continued until Reagan and Gorbachev agreed to remove certain missiles from Europe, the Soviet Union collapsed, and the cold war ended. This is where Holloway ends his story, but the nuclear saga he describes continues as Russia, the US, and now China build and modernize deadly nuclear weapons that each hopes will keep the others in check.

Finally, in Truth and Consequence: Reflections on Catastrophe, Civil Resistance, and Hope, we get a bracing moral perspective from the voluminous private notes and writings of Daniel Ellsberg, as compiled by his son Michael Ellsberg and his longtime assistant Jan Thomas. Although better known for leaking the Pentagon Papers during the Vietnam War, Ellsberg was one of the “whiz kids” in the national security world of the 1950s and 1960s and worked directly with the principal architects of US nuclear policy. At the Pentagon, Ellsberg, with his top-level security clearance, had access to America’s nuclear attack plans.

In his book The Doomsday Machine: Confessions of a Nuclear War Planner (2017), he recounts first seeing an Eisenhower administration document called SIOP-62 in the spring of 1961, soon after his thirtieth birthday. It envisioned, in the event of war, launching as many as 3,200 nuclear warheads against the Soviet Union, China, and the other communist countries. Without even fully accounting for radioactive fallout, the expected death toll was in the hundreds of millions. From that day forward, Ellsberg tells us, he “had one overriding life purpose: to prevent the execution of any such plan.”

His writings give a window into the thinking of a man who faced the insanity of nuclear weapons without flinching. On nuclear deterrence and its inherent threat of annihilation, Ellsberg writes, “Merely as risk-taking it has been an unbearably reckless, evil gamble.” By comparison, Brad Roberts, President Barack Obama’s policy director for the Nuclear Posture Review, wrote, “Part of the answer is to update the menu of potential options for reducing risk in light of the risk net assessment framework described above.” Ellsberg counters, “Any nuclear plan is a plan for madness. I am living in a society that is preparing a catastrophe. I taste ashes in the wind.”

Truth and Consequence offers a glimpse of Ellsberg’s courageous and eventful life—how his mother forced him to practice the piano for endless hours because she wanted him to be a concert pianist, how she and his sister died in an automobile crash that he and his father survived, his service in the Marine Corps, his loyalty to America and the president, and his realization that the Vietnam War was wrong and American nuclear policies deranged. In these pages we learn why an insider exposed to shocking secrets at the heart of US policy left government service to become a lifelong activist and risked life in prison to reveal official lies and deception.

“Why did I never hear anyone raise the question, ‘Is this right?’” Ellsberg wonders. “Why were ethical or moral principles never mentioned? The only questions raised were: Will this work? Is it expedient? Is it worth the risk? Will we get away with it?” He adds:

For 25 years I have been trying to understand, so as to prevent, a catastrophe: nuclear war.

How could this possibility have been permitted? The very possibility of murder on this scale, which seems unmistakably real, is a mystery that I am trying to investigate: a mass murder mystery.

These warnings have gone unheeded. In 2023 the Congressional Commission on the Strategic Posture of the United States—a twelve-member bipartisan panel of national security experts—fully endorsed the nuclear modernization program, now estimated to cost at least $1.7 trillion, and called for an even bigger buildup. This includes more of everything: B-21 bombers and tanker aircraft, long-range air-launched cruise missiles, Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missiles with multiple warheads, Columbia-class ballistic missile submarines, a new “theater” nuclear delivery system for deployment to Asia and Europe, and much else.

In addition to taking up many of these proposals, Congress is now considering Trump’s Golden Dome, a trillion-dollar scheme to place an ineffective missile defense “shield” over the entire country. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that to destroy just ten incoming ballistic missiles would cost $720 billion. The idea that the Golden Dome could reliably knock out hundreds, even thousands of missiles is preposterous. But the existence of an American nuclear shield, however flawed, would be perceived by Russia as part of a US plan to attack with impunity. This would dramatically increase tension between Russia and the US and reduce, not increase, American security. Russia’s stockpile of more than five thousand warheads matches America’s, and Russia is now building systems that could penetrate whatever nuclear defenses the US constructs.4

China’s own buildup makes this an unprecedented three-way competition. Already, according to Pentagon estimates, it has doubled its nuclear arsenal from three hundred warheads in 2020 to more than six hundred in 2025, with the goal to produce one thousand by 2030. This new dynamic of three competing powers makes nuclear restraint increasingly unlikely as each country attempts to match the others. Furthermore, six other countries have the bomb—Great Britain, France, India, Pakistan, Israel, and North Korea—and are expanding their capacity. The unsettled wars in Ukraine and Iran add to the instability. Putin has made veiled nuclear threats, has launched nuclear-capable missiles, and is reportedly considering escalating the conflict against European nations that support Ukraine. Meanwhile, Trump is threatening to resume nuclear testing for the first time since 1992.

Scientific knowledge and technology continue to advance. Our ability to reduce, much less eliminate, the nuclear threat has not. Our leaders are complacent or distracted with respect to the risks of nuclear horror. They are men driven by grievance and whim. The public is uninformed or else desensitized. The antinuclear movement that engaged millions in the 1980s does not exist today. The cycle of distrust and competition intensifies.

Ellsberg died in June 2023. A few months before, he and I spent several hours talking at his home in Kensington, California, a small community not far from San Francisco. Despite his terminal cancer diagnosis, he was cheerful and at peace. He reflected on his life’s effort to rid the world of nuclear weapons and bluntly acknowledged his failure. Then, without a trace of irony or exaggeration, he compared our current course to that of the Titanic, speeding through the dark despite numerous ice warnings. His message was clear: we are not merely drifting toward Armageddon, we are racing there.

entries.content:
As blood is brought where infection is

So was I brought to Los Angeles

Toting only my REI membership card

And University of California ID

“Access the inaccessible”

My headlamp quibbled

But I didn’t need its LEDs

To see them, the coyotes,

Rip the heads from Griffin’s chickens

In broad daylight when I’d let them out to graze

Because Griffin told me to because

He’d made a calculation

Their freedom of movement

Was worth the risk of death, certain

Though it seemed to me, even when the coyotes

Left the necks intact, bleeding

And I had Mike come over and finish the job

And I just watched and it was and was not

Like the news, it wasn’t like watching the news

At all, but it helped me understand the news

entries.title: The Slave’s Power
entries.summary: Two recent books employ inventive approaches to read against the grain of the archive of slavery produced by those who built and benefited from it.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
For nearly two decades now, historians have been debating whether it is even possible to write the history of American slavery. Can an accurate story of a system of oppression be derived from sources created and preserved by the oppressors? In many ways it is a surprising controversy. For the generation of American historians working after the emergence of the mainstream civil rights movement in the mid-1950s, slavery studies represented perhaps the most exciting field of American historical scholarship, attracting an audience of general readers as well as the attention of prominent academics. Books about slavery were discussed in popular magazines and featured on the nightly news. Innovative methodologies, including demography and quantitative analysis, folklore, material culture, oral history, and family reconstitution opened new windows into the past. At the same time, changed assumptions about racial equality made the “moonlight and magnolias” South of Gone with the Wind and most earlier studies of slavery obsolete. Historians began to construct a rich and sobering narrative of the lives of both enslavers and enslaved, as well as a portrait of the system that bound them together.

It seems even odder to be having this debate now, when attacks on history by the right demand that such matters as chattel slavery be erased altogether or reconfigured to ensure an adequately “patriotic” account of the national past. Last year, several weeks after President Donald Trump instructed the Smithsonian Institution that it would have to adjust anything his administration took issue with regarding “tone, historical framing and alignment with American ideals,” he complained that the Smithsonian’s museums focused too much on “how bad Slavery was.” The National Park Service is revising interpretations at its sites to offer an upbeat rendering of human bondage, if slavery is mentioned at all. In January Park Service workers took crowbars to signage memorializing the nine enslaved people who worked in George Washington’s presidential house in Philadelphia.1 We have never needed more to believe in—and defend—the possibility of a rigorous, fact-based telling of slavery’s history. Our nation’s future requires a clear-eyed understanding of how its aspirations for freedom and democracy coexisted with an institution defined by violence and injustice. We cannot overcome our past if we fail to document and confront it, and so we must strive to make the realities of American slavery ever more visible and undeniable.

But can we adequately document an institution whose records were overwhelmingly produced by those who built and benefited from it? In her presidential address to the American Historical Association in January 2025, Thavolia Glymph, a professor of history at Duke, insisted that this is not just a possibility but a necessity. She challenged those who assail what historians have come to call the “archive” of slavery—the manuscripts and books left by our forebears—as too compromised to be useful. Critics have argued that this record, the creation of enslavers and white supremacists, reflects the interests of the empowered and silences the enslaved, who were mostly prohibited from reading and writing and thus left unable to tell their side of the story.2 Glymph readily admitted that this is the “damaged space that we historians have to work with.” Yet even with its biases she said she finds it “boisterous” and “noisy,” full of unruly voices of the subjugated, awaiting the historian’s discerning eye. Every encounter with power, she insisted, “also captures the agitation of the enslaved that led to the encounter.” In their effort to control the archive, enslavers did “a pretty bad job; indeed, they failed miserably.” Glymph’s own deeply researched work on enslaved and formerly enslaved women is testimony to her argument.3 “Millions of paper tracings,” she said, “are there in which enslaved people claim for themselves more than a trace in history.”

Two recent books represent the remarkable discoveries that this archive of slavery can yield. Both recognize the distortions inherent in a record kept by those who defended human bondage and believed that Black people are inferior. Yet both employ inventive approaches to read against the grain of the nineteenth-century materials available to them. And each is clearly caught up in the spirit of the hunt and the joy of searching for hidden treasures that inspire the best historical researchers.

A professor at the University of Memphis, Susan Eva O’Donovan has immersed herself in what she embraces as “slavery’s vast archive,” exploring “correspondence, ledgers, diaries, logs, receipts, reports, contracts, complaints, bills, court cases, police blotters, and ship manifests” in order to reconstruct the experience of human bondage. At the outset of her career, more than thirty years ago, O’Donovan served as an assistant editor at the Freedmen and Southern Society Project, a pathbreaking initiative established in 1976 to identify materials relevant to the coming of freedom, chiefly in the voluminous holdings of the National Archives. No one had systematically looked for such documents before or asked the questions about the African American past that by the 1970s had come to be seen as essential. The FSSP has in the years since published six doorstop volumes of evidence about slavery and emancipation. O’Donovan is a coeditor of two (and Glymph coeditor of two others). Few historians are more familiar with the records of American slavery and the opportunities for writing its history.

Advertisement

Her purpose in Moving Toward Freedom: The Political Education of Enslaved Americans is to demonstrate that even before emancipation the enslaved had carved out spaces of independence from their enslavers. In the years leading up to the Civil War, Black southerners were not simply victims of oppression but also a people in motion—literally across land and water and figuratively toward freedom, even when an end to slavery seemed all but unimaginable. Masters’ control was never absolute, and slaves exploited these limitations, readying themselves to take advantage of their eventual legal emancipation. Theirs was, she insists, the work of politics, an assertion of power not at a ballot box but through the events and arrangements of everyday life. O’Donovan’s arguments build on earlier work by a number of other scholars who identified a Black politics that emerged even under slavery, perhaps most notably Steven Hahn’s A Nation Under Our Feet: Black Political Struggles in the Rural South from Slavery to the Great Migration, which won the Pulitzer Prize in History in 2004. But the richness of her examples and her use of the lens of motion and travel succeed in deepening our understanding.

The balance of oppression and resistance in slavery is complex, O’Donovan stresses. To overemphasize the agency of the enslaved would be to “ignore the violent character of American slavery, an institution forged to steal the labor of millions for white people’s gain.” But to minimize the influence of slaves within the system of constraints imposed on them would be yet another subjugation. The enslaved were, to borrow the parlance of the civil rights movement, “making a way out of no way.”

O’Donovan centers her analysis on examples of slaves moving beyond their places of bondage in the regular course of doing their owners’ business. The tension between freedom and total control, she shows, lies at the very heart of what southerners called “the peculiar institution.” Using unfree workers optimally and efficiently often required granting them some modicum of autonomy, some reprieve from constant scrutiny, some access to the world beyond the master’s direct purview. “To leash their laborers too tightly,” she writes, “would be to strangle themselves and their great golden goose.” Enslaved men worked as crews and as skilled pilots and stewards on steamboats, and as loggers and “wooders” providing fuel along inland waterways. On land, enslaved teamsters hauled goods—for example, cotton to market—similarly escaping the “suffocating surveillance” of the plantation. Their travels put them in contact with people from other parts of the nation and beyond, often in situations in which sharp social and racial distinctions were difficult to uphold and new ideas, including those that might challenge slavery, difficult to suppress. As the Missouri Supreme Court wrote in an 1835 case involving an enslaved drayman, “He acts as a freeman all the day.”

The movement of enslaved women tended to have a different character. Many traveled as domestic servants for the convenience of their mistresses, visiting spas like Saratoga Springs in New York or cities like Philadelphia or even London where slavery did not exist. O’Donovan ingeniously uses a federal record of all enslaved people who left or entered United States’ seaports, a register kept after 1808 to monitor possible violations of the law banning the international slave trade. She finds that such travelers were overwhelmingly female—in most cases, she argues, the attendants of elite southerners visiting abroad or embarking on the grand tour. Their journeys introduced them to new worlds. On a transatlantic steamship voyage, Frederick Douglass remarked that “all color distinctions were flung to the winds.” Enslaved workers who had witnessed free societies and seen the place of free African Americans within them no longer understood their own situation as unalterable. Travel helped produce a contagion of liberty.

Over the course of the antebellum era, boom and bust could accelerate or diminish mobility. In the 1820s and 1830s, expansion into the cotton kingdom of the Old Southwest—Alabama, Mississippi, Arkansas, and other states—relocated hundreds of thousands of Black southerners who were transported or sold to cultivate rich virgin soils. In the 1850s high cotton prices drove productivity, which in turn required more marketing and hauling, more teamsters and enslaved workers interacting with towns and cities beyond their plantations.

Advertisement

Moments of genuine activism emerged out of growing political awareness among the enslaved as sectional hostilities and attacks on slavery intensified. Anxious slaveholders worried about the “great meetings” of their unfree laborers that began during John C. Frémont’s Free Soil campaign for the presidency in 1856. O’Donovan describes protests that erupted along a canal in Rockbridge, Virginia, and along a railroad under construction in Alabama, as well as a rebellion plotted in a plantation district near Memphis. In South Carolina, a committee of slaves sent a delegation to the governor to petition for “redress of certain grievances.” As one Black southerner later recalled, in the years after the 1856 election “a great anger arose among the colored people,” and they “began to study how they would get free.”

When Union armies advanced into the South in 1861, enslaved people knew what was at stake. Some hundreds of thousands fled to Union lines because, O’Donovan argues, they had been “laying the foundations for liberation for decades.” They were ready, and they understood, in the words of an 1865 petition of the Black residents of Nashville, “the burdens of citizenship” as well as its promises. As a gathering of freedpeople declared to Union general Joseph Fullerton in July 1865, “We is come to the law now.”

In A Terrible Intimacy: Interracial Life in the Slaveholding South, Melvin Patrick Ely, a professor at William and Mary, makes clear that Black southerners had in fact been touched by the law throughout the antebellum period. Unlike O’Donovan’s sweeping study, Ely’s book is sharply focused, delving into six criminal cases in one Virginia community—the notorious Prince Edward County, which achieved an enduring place in history by closing its public schools from 1959 until 1964 rather than integrating them after the Supreme Court’s Brown v. Board of Education decision.

Yet like O’Donovan, Ely relishes the relentless quest for sources, and his excitement is evident in discoveries like the “sheaf of bluish-brown tissue-thin pages” recording the testimony at an 1854 rape trial or the rare court minute book he found in a little-used archival warehouse near the Richmond airport. He offers the reader a you-are-there approach both to his own work as a scholar and to the proceedings of a nineteenth-century courtroom.

Ely seeks to particularize the history of slavery, to embed it in the stories of individual men and women, white and Black, whose testimony, “not verbatim but very detailed,” was recorded by court clerks. Such sources have often been dismissed as partial and unreliable evidence because of laws that prohibited Black people from testifying against white defendants in southern states. But Ely shows us how much was said in spite of this prohibition, citing examples of white people on the stand relating stories they had heard from African Americans—a confounding judicial circumstance in which the admission of hearsay in some measure compensated for the limits on Black testimony. And Black people, both free and enslaved, who were not themselves on trial were frequent witnesses (if the defendant was not white) and were recorded speaking at length.

Ely, too, emphasizes the complexity of slavery as a system and as a web of human relationships. In Prince Edward County, three quarters of white households owned slaves, but in small numbers, not in large plantation-scale holdings. It was, Ely writes, “a little republic of middle-level slaveholding men” that thrust people together across class and race and condition—even in court. The “terrible intimacy” of his title refers to the closeness of Black and white people in nearly every aspect of daily life, including sexual ties across the color line and blurred family links that defied notions of racial purity. But this was, as he describes it, a “deformed” intimacy produced by a society “that exploited and abused” Black people.

To enable his readers to engage directly with the past themselves, Ely organizes his book around the reports of witness testimony for the six cases he uses to capture his slice of nineteenth-century southern life. His earlier works, he explains, simply presented his interpretation of his sources from the perspective of an omniscient narrator; he effectively asked the reader to “trust me.” But this time “I want you to walk through these stories with me—to see them unfold as they did in the community and then in the courtroom.” He adopts a familiar, conversational tone, assessing what he sees, acknowledging where he finds the record “biased and riddled with blind spots,” and using his extensive knowledge of the place and the period to help make sense of materials that might otherwise seem puzzling. Each trial unfolds step by step, often revealing surprising twists that underscore the contradictory forces of humanity and inhumanity in the everyday life of a slave society.

An enslaved man named George is acquitted of rape in an 1854 trial in which his white accuser’s lower-class status and dubious reputation sway the jury to credit the supportive testimony of white witnesses. Mary Tatum was regarded by her neighbors with contempt; George seemed always appropriately “straight-forward humble & obedient.” As one elderly white woman explained, “I thought the negro ought not to be hung for nothing.” In a murder trial in 1861, after the outbreak of the Civil War, witnesses tell a sickening tale of cruelty inflicted on William, a man accused of killing his enslaver. The prisoner is not executed but instead convicted of second-degree murder, with his sentence commuted by the governor to life at labor on public works. Yet in the course of testimony it becomes evident that many white members of the community had long known of this owner’s “very barbarous” behavior—extracting teeth as punishment, beating William so frequently that his back became a giant scab. Yet they did nothing until their neighbor was dead and William on trial.

The southern system of slavery hid under the veneer of law, but Ely illustrates the elusiveness of genuine justice or mercy within its structures of repression. Human beings both Black and white nevertheless pushed the limits of control, motivated by a wide range of factors—pure self-interest in the case of enslavers who did not want to lose their valuable slave property to the gallows, human sympathy from individuals connected to one another even across racial lines, as well as Black Virginians’ anticipation that white people might somehow, someday be called to account as Christians and Americans.

O’Donovan notes that more than two hundred Black men and women who had been taken outside the South for a period of time by their enslavers sued for freedom in the same court that heard the famous case of Dred Scott, all arguing that once they had set foot on free soil they were legally free. Ely offers no example of such direct use of the law by African Americans in Prince Edward County. But even as the enslaved people who came into that Virginia courtroom were subjected to the display of white supremacy, they also confronted some of its weaknesses, likely emboldening them to seize their freedom when the moment arrived. Rife with the contradictions inherent in defining human beings as chattel property, slavery contained the germs of its own destruction, and both authors let us understand how those seeds might have taken root.

Did William, sentenced in 1861, labor on the public works for life? Or did he run to Union lines when Northern troops advanced and provided an opportunity? Even Ely’s prodigious research gives us no answer to these questions. The archive of slavery cannot tell us all we would like to know. But it can tell us a great deal, and it can continue to challenge us to reckon with a national past that represents human failures as well as human triumphs. We today are the products of all of those. A crowbar cannot change that.
